operator, a higher top line, and demand spread more evenly across the week, which eases
staffing. A null result, that a category's environmental footprint does not predict its
uplift, is reported as a finding against an intuitive expectation. The research
implications place the paper in three marketing conversations: retail performance,
keeping physical stores relevant, and sustainability-oriented marketing. The published
version also carries an approved alternative disclosure plan, with proprietary data and
disguised data and code deposited with the journal's Data Editor, which is how a paper
built on one retailer's books meets JMR's replication policy.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Arguing for an effect someone else found first

1. Name the decision maker whose question this is, and choose the outcome that answers
   that question, even if it means excluding revenue the treatment also produces.
2. Treat earlier estimates as a baseline to sharpen. Tie each design difference to a
   specific bias or blind spot in the earlier measures, never to "better data" in
   general.
3. Ground the gap in what earlier data could not show, and quote the earlier authors'
   own calls for future research when they exist.
4. Put the positioning in a table a reviewer can audit at a glance.
5. Argue exogeneity from the process that sets the treatment date, then test each way
   that argument could fail.
6. If no mediator is measured on the right units at the right frequency, decompose the
   outcome and rerun the Stage 1 design on each component.
7. Report the difference test for every split, and keep the summary sentence in the
   same register as the table behind it.
8. End each contribution with the person who can act on it, and price it in that
   person's currency.
:::

### A Third Specimen: Mechanism by Moderation, Without a Model {#sec-sw-emb-listings}

@luca2026gettingmap, published in *Management Science* in 2026 (marketing department),
ask whether being listed on a review platform raises a small business's revenue. Their
answer is 5% to 10% for Texas bars and restaurants added to Yelp. The paper is worth
studying for its craft more than its topic. It builds all three stages from reduced-form
evidence, with no structural demand model and no formal theory model. It also runs on
an outcome anyone can download (@sec-data-txmb). The account below draws its numbers
from the NBER working-paper version [@luca2022gettingmapwp]. The heterogeneity results
summarized at the end are from the published abstract, because the working paper does
not yet contain them.

**The main effect is set up by a descriptive puzzle.** The paper's first result is a
count, not a coefficient. About 18% of alcohol-serving establishments in the state still
had no listing at the end of 2017, and 4,810 of 14,381 were never listed at all, even
though a listing costs nothing. That fact does two jobs. It makes the causal question
non-obvious: if a free listing raised revenue, why would so many owners skip it? It also
sets the extensive margin apart from the review literature, which had studied ratings,
rankings, and review counts for businesses already on the platform. The working paper
then gives the magnitude a familiar benchmark, comparing it with the revenue value of
one additional star.

**The endogeneity argument is a ladder, and each rung removes the owner from the timing
decision.** The threat is specific: an owner might add a listing during a renovation,
an ownership change, or an upswing, and the revenue gain would then belong to those
events. The paper answers with four samples, each estimated with the same imputation
difference-in-differences and establishment and county-by-month fixed effects
(@fig-sw-listings-ladder). The estimate is 0.052 log points for all listings and 0.052 for
venues listed at least three months after opening, which rules out a new-venue ramp-up.
It is 0.089 for the 747 venues listed by 56 "super-adders", the top 1% of users by
listings created, whose timing has nothing to do with the restaurant's plans. It is
0.104 for the 1,295 venues Yelp created on 22 and 23 July 2010 from a purchased directory
file, whose timing the platform set. The direction of travel is the argument. If owner
timing inflated the full-sample estimate, taking the owner out should shrink it. It
grows instead. Event-study leads close the case by showing no rise in revenue before any
listing.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-sw-listings-ladder
%%| fig-cap: "The identification ladder in the working paper on online listings. Each rung moves the choice of listing date further from the owner, and the estimated revenue effect rises rather than falls."
flowchart LR
  R1["All listings<br/>date set by owners,<br/>users, or platform<br/>+0.052"] --> R2["Listed 3+ months<br/>after opening<br/>no new-venue ramp<br/>+0.052"]
  R2 --> R3["Added by 56<br/>super-adders<br/>date set by heavy users<br/>+0.089"]
  R3 --> R4["Bulk adds, July 2010<br/>date set by a<br/>data purchase<br/>+0.104"]
```

Two qualifications show what each rung costs. First, every rung changes the population
as well as the identification. Bulk-added venues are more rural (75% urban against 86%
for all listed venues) and later earn a mean rating of 2.09 against 3.03. So the 0.104 is
an effect for the kind of venue that waits to be added, not a cleaner estimate of the
0.052. The ladder supports "positive, and not an artifact of owner timing". It does not
support a single number. Second, the estimator is part of the evidence. Ordinary
two-way fixed effects give 0.054 for the bulk sample, about half the two-stage estimate.
The paper explains its choice by its setting: the panel is unbalanced in calendar time,
and Yelp's reach grows over the sample, so effects should differ by when a venue was
listed. That is the case in which the robust estimators of @sec-causal-week06 matter.
The two-way results go in an appendix, so a reader can see the gap.

**Measurement is validated where it could fail.** Two of the paper's inputs are proxies,
and each gets its own check. Alcohol receipts stand in for total revenue, and an appendix
assembles outside evidence that the two move together. The tax-to-Yelp match comes from
Yelp's internal matcher, which the authors audited with three crowdworkers per venue on
750 venues. Of the matched venues, 241 of 250 really were on Yelp. Of the unmatched
venues, 202 of 250 really were absent. The second number deserves more weight than the
working paper gives it. The paper says only false positives affect its regressions, but
never-listed venues are its main control group. A listed venue misclassified as
unlisted therefore sits among the controls, and with about one unmatched venue in five
actually listed, the bias runs toward zero.

**The mechanism comes from who gains, not from a mediator.** The first specimen measured
a mediator, and the second decomposed the outcome. This paper takes a third route, and
it is the one open to anyone without a mediator series. Each candidate mechanism
predicts which venues should gain more. If a listing works by standing in for reputation
the venue cannot build otherwise, gains should be larger where reputation is hard to
build: independents rather than chains, and tourist areas whose customers lack local
knowledge. If a listing works by revealing quality to people who would not otherwise
see it, gains should be larger for better products. The published abstract reports both
patterns. Independents and venues in tourist areas gain more, and so do larger venues
and those with good reviews. Each split is a prediction stated before the table, so the
heterogeneity table is the mechanism test. A disclosure result answers the opening
puzzle. Venues that stayed off the platform until the bulk import earned lower ratings,
as voluntary-disclosure models predict: owners who expect bad reviews have a reason not
to list. Even so, they gained from being listed.

The honesty requirement applies with full force here, because no one randomized chain
status. A chain-versus-independent split is also a split by size, location, and
management. Moderation evidence is consistent with a mechanism. It does not isolate one.
Its strongest form, which this design reaches toward, pairs splits on which rival
mechanisms predict opposite signs, so that only one story fits the whole pattern.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Explaining an effect without a model

1. Open with the descriptive fact that makes the causal question puzzling (here, free
   listings that many owners skip).
2. Name who chooses the treatment date, and build a ladder of samples in which someone
   progressively further from the outcome chooses it.
3. Read the ladder by the direction its estimates move, and say what population each
   rung represents.
4. Justify the estimator from features of the setting (unbalanced panel, effects that
   grow with the platform), and show the naive estimator in an appendix.
5. Audit every constructed variable, and work out which group each error type
   contaminates.
6. Derive from each candidate mechanism a prediction about who gains more, state it
   before the table, and treat the heterogeneity table as the mechanism test.
7. Use the selection result (who stayed out) to answer the puzzle you opened with.
:::

The template transfers directly to studies of firms adopting a free digital channel,
such as opening a social media account, joining a marketplace, or claiming a profile.
Each shares the three problems this paper solves. The adopter picks the date, the
non-adopters are a selected group worth describing in their own right, and the outcome
has to come from outside the platform, or the effect of being on the platform is measured
with the platform's own data. The rung to look for is an adoption whose date someone
other than the firm set. Tax receipts, permits, and other administrative records solve
the outcome problem when they exist, and @sec-data-txmb shows what one such source
takes to use.

### A Fourth Specimen: A Small Reward Framed as Four Open Questions {#sec-sw-emb-plasma}

@bruers2026plasma, published online in *Management Science* in 2026, is about as plain
as a field experiment gets. Four of twelve Red Cross-Flanders donation centers gave
plasma donors one extra thank-you coupon, worth about €1.50, for six months. There is
no structural model, no instrument, and no machine learning. The paper is worth reading
for how a modest manipulation became a contribution a general-interest journal would
take. It fits the three-stage architecture loosely. There is a randomized effect,
boundaries in time and across behaviors, and a mechanism stage built from a survey.
Published estimates below come from the article's abstract. Design details and
month-by-month estimates come from the KU Leuven dissertation chapter that first
reported the experiment [@bruers2024thesis]. Where the two versions differ, we say so.

**One experiment, four questions.** The dissertation chapter asked a collector's
question: how cost-effective are small material rewards for plasma donors? The
published version asks four questions about prosocial behavior in general. Each is
answered by a single feature of the design (@tbl-sw-plasma-questions). This is the move
most worth copying. A narrower paper would bury the information-only arm, the
month-by-month estimates, and the blood-donation outcome as robustness checks. Here
each becomes a headline result, because each answers a question the literature had
left open.

| Open question | Why a reader cannot guess the answer | Design feature that answers it | Published answer |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Do small rewards motivate prosocial behavior? | A payment small enough to seem token can lower effort below no payment at all [@gneezy2000payenough] | An extra coupon worth about €1.50, added to an existing coupon scheme | Plasma donations rise 7.1% over the reward period |
| How do short-run effects differ from longer-run adjustment? | Earlier randomized donor-incentive experiments ran for much shorter treatment periods | A 24-month donor panel: 11 months before treatment, 9 under it, 4 after | The reward effect grows over six months and disappears once the coupon is withdrawn |
| Do incentives pull effort away from other prosocial activities? | Displacement had been measured across nearby blood drives [@lacetera2012blood], not across the products one donor can give | Centers collect both blood and plasma, and only plasma earns the extra coupon | Blood donations fall 3.3% |
| Do reminders about existing rewards matter? | Donors may not know which coupons they already receive | A separate arm whose newsletter only states the existing coupons | Plasma donations rise 4.6% over nine months, an effect that fades with repetition |

: The anatomy of the framing in @bruers2026plasma. Questions and answers follow the published abstract. The second and third columns draw on the dissertation chapter's review and design [@bruers2024thesis]. {#tbl-sw-plasma-questions}

Each question also passes the test of @sec-sw-open-question: both answers would have
been publishable. A null on the first question would be evidence of crowding-out. A
drop below baseline after the coupon was withdrawn would have been a backlash result.
Zero substitution would mean the gain was net. The paper did not need any particular
sign to have a contribution, which is what made a small experiment safe to run for two
years.

**The long panel turns a small effect into a dynamics story.** @fig-sw-plasma-timeline
shows the schedule. The reward arm received the newsletter item for three months
before its extra coupon began, to accustom donors to seeing the coupons stated. Every
change was announced a month ahead. That staggering separates the reminder from the
reward within a single arm. The dissertation's monthly estimates trace the shape. The
reward effect climbs from 6.4% in January 2023 to 9.8% in June. The information effect
peaks at about 8% in the second and third months and falls to 0.8% by the ninth. The
versions disagree on one point. The dissertation reports a 4.4% effect in the first
month after withdrawal, which then fades. The published abstract says the effect
disappears immediately. Quote the version you cite.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-sw-plasma-timeline
%%| fig-cap: "The schedule of the plasma-reward experiment, from the dissertation chapter, with the effects the published abstract reports. Both treated arms received the newsletter item for nine months; only the reward arm received the third coupon, for the last six."
flowchart LR
  P["Pre-period<br/>Nov 2021 to Sep 2022<br/>11 months, no treatment"] --> I["Information only<br/>Oct to Dec 2022<br/>newsletter states the coupons<br/>in both treated arms"]
  I --> R["Reward period<br/>Jan to Jun 2023<br/>reward arm: 3 coupons<br/>for plasma instead of 2"]
  R --> Q["Post-period<br/>Jul to Oct 2023<br/>2 coupons again,<br/>no newsletter item"]
  I -.-> E1["Reminder: +4.6%<br/>over nine months,<br/>fading with repetition"]
  R -.-> E2["Extra coupon: +7.1% plasma,<br/>growing; blood -3.3%"]
  Q -.-> E3["Reward effect gone<br/>(published version)"]
```

The dissertation's appendix prints the monthly donation counts for each center, so the
picture can be redrawn from the page. @fig-sw-plasma-dynamics redraws it and fits the
dissertation's center-level robustness model: log monthly donations on center and month
fixed effects plus the two treatment indicators.

```{r}
  ), nrow = 24, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(NULL, centers))
month <- -10:13   # month 1 = October 2022, the first newsletter that states the coupons

# Each treated arm's total relative to the control arm, rescaled so that the
# eleven pre-experiment months average 1 (the dissertation's Figure 38).
arm_total <- sapply(split(seq_along(centers), arm), function(j) rowSums(plasma[, j]))
relative  <- arm_total[, c("information", "reward")] / arm_total[, "control"]
relative  <- sweep(relative, 2, colMeans(relative[month <= 0, ]), "/")

plot(month, relative[, "reward"], type = "n", ylim = c(0.93, 1.18),
     xlab = "Month (1 = October 2022)", ylab = "Plasma donations relative to control",
     main = "Information decays; the extra coupon builds, then stops")
rect(0.5, 0, 9.5, 2, col = "grey92", border = NA)   # newsletter states the coupons
rect(3.5, 0, 9.5, 2, col = "grey82", border = NA)   # reward arm: third coupon
abline(h = 1, lty = 3)
lines(month, relative[, "information"], type = "b", pch = 1, lty = 2)
lines(month, relative[, "reward"], type = "b", pch = 16)
legend("topleft", c("Information arm", "Information + reward arm"),
       pch = c(1, 16), lty = c(2, 1), bty = "n")

# The dissertation's center-level robustness model: log donations on center and
# month fixed effects plus the two treatment indicators.
d <- data.frame(month = rep(month, 12), center = rep(centers, each = 24),
                arm = rep(arm, each = 24), donations = as.vector(plasma))
d$information <- as.integer(d$arm != "control" & d$month %in% 1:9)
d$reward      <- as.integer(d$arm == "reward"  & d$month %in% 4:9)
fit <- lm(log(donations) ~ factor(month) + factor(center) + information + reward, data = d)
round(100 * (exp(coef(fit)[c("information", "reward")]) - 1), 1)   # percent effects
```

Plain least squares on the transcribed table gives 3.6% for the information item and
6.0% for the reward. For this model the dissertation reports 3.3% and 5.5%, fitted with
autocorrelated errors that we did not reproduce. Its preferred donor-level
fixed-effects Poisson model gives 4.6% and 7.1%, the figures the published abstract
carries. The figure also shows why the donor-level model carries the paper. With four
centers per arm, the pre-period ratios wander by up to about five percent either side
of 1. Month 0, before any treatment, already sits near 1.06 in both arms. The late
spike in month 13 comes from a recruitment campaign, which the dissertation notes
worked best at the two largest centers, both in treated arms.

**Substitution is priced, not just reported.** The partner collects blood and plasma at
the same sites, so the experiment can see what the coupon costs in the prosocial act it
did not reward. In the dissertation's numbers, the blood decline is barely significant
at the donor level (p = 0.047) and not significant in the center-level model. It
accounts for about one sixth of the plasma gain. The paper reports it anyway, and the
cost arithmetic shows why. Every plasma donor gets the extra coupon, including those
who would have come anyway. The dissertation therefore puts the marginal cost at
€1.50 × 107% / 7%, about €23 per extra plasma donation, and €34 once the lost blood
donations are netted out. The same dissertation's meta-analysis puts the cost of cash
or vouchers worth €5 to €15 per blood donation at €20 to €120 per extra donation. A
cost per net extra donation is the number a collector can act on.

**The partner shapes the design, and the paper says how.** The Red Cross funded the
study and supplied administrative records on 77,646 donors who gave at a center at
least once over the two years. The outcome is therefore a count of donations, not a
stated intention. The partner's rules also set the design's limits. An informal cap of
about €5 on rewards for voluntary, unpaid donation limited the reward to three coupons.
A rule against treating donors at the same center differently meant that centers, not
donors, were randomized. The twelve centers were grouped by cluster analysis into four
triplets of similar size and donor mix, and one center per triplet went to each arm.
Matching helps, but twelve units cannot balance everything: 43% of control-arm donors
lived more than 15 km from their center, against 26% in each treated arm. Inference is
the other cost. The dissertation clusters standard errors by donor, although treatment
varies by center. With twelve clusters, a referee will ask for center-level inference
such as the wild cluster bootstrap (@sec-causal-week05). Say in the paper what the
partner allowed and what it cost.

**Registration, described accurately.** The trial appears in the AEA RCT Registry
[@bruers2024registry], but the entry was submitted in August 2024, more than a year
after the intervention ended in June 2023. The dissertation states that no
preregistration was done, while noting that the models and hypotheses were fixed
before data collection. A registration filed after the data exist documents a design.
It does not constrain the analysis the way a pre-analysis plan does, and a careful
reader will check the dates. Describe your own registration by its date.

**A mechanism stage without a model.** The dissertation closed by asking whether a
larger reward works through donors' self-interest or by signaling that donations are
more urgently needed. The published version answers with survey evidence. Small
rewards act as signals of increased need or as gifts that call for reciprocity, and
the authors suggest the findings may carry over to volunteering. The survey's design is
not described in the versions we could read. Asking recipients how they interpret an
incentive is a cheap mechanism stage, and the honesty requirement applies to it in
full: stated interpretations are consistent with a mechanism but do not isolate one.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Making a small field experiment publishable

1. Turn the one effect into several open questions, and give each a design feature
   that answers it.
2. Write each question so that either answer is a result, including a null.
3. Run the panel long enough to see build-up, decay, and what happens after the
   treatment ends, and report effects month by month.
4. Measure the behavior the incentive might pull people away from, and fold the loss
   into the cost per unit gained.
5. Give reminding people of what they already get its own arm, separate from giving
   them more.
6. Use the partner's administrative outcomes, and state which of the partner's rules
   shaped the design.
7. Match inference to the unit of randomization, and say how many clusters you have.
8. Date your registration honestly, and add a direct check on mechanism, even a
   survey, before a referee asks for one.
:::

The template carries over to loyalty programs and promotions. A points bonus on one
product line is the same experiment, and substitution away from the other lines is the
outcome that keeps the estimate honest.

### A Fifth Specimen: One Effect, Several Routes {#sec-sw-emb-roads}

@agarwal2026road, published in *Management Science* in 2026 (finance department), ask
whether building a rural road brings a village's households into the stock market. The
treatment and the outcome sit far apart, and a reader's first reaction is to ask how
asphalt could open a brokerage account. That distance is why the paper is useful here.
The main effect takes one table. Most of the paper is spent on the routes from road to
trade, and each route gets its own prediction, its own data source, and its own test.
The earlier specimens each explained an effect one way: a mediator, a decomposition, a
moderator table, a survey. This one runs several explanations side by side and tries to
discriminate among them.

The account below is drawn from the February 2022 working paper [@agarwal2022roadwp],
because the published text was not accessible when this section was written. Where the
published abstract differs, the difference is noted. Magnitudes need particular care.
The February 2022 draft reports that a new road raises the number of new investors in a
postal code by 28.7% and their trades by 64.5%. The abstract on record for the SSRN
version reports 6.8% and 7.9%, and the published abstract reports no magnitude. The
numbers below are the 2022 draft's and show the pattern of the argument. Take
magnitudes from the published tables before quoting any.

**The setting supplies the design, and the paper borrows it openly.** India's rural road
program (PMGSY) built all-weather feeder roads to more than 115,000 previously
unconnected villages. Development economists had already used the program to study
schooling, labor, and lending, and the paper says it follows the empirical strategy
of one of those studies. The new ingredient is the outcome: every trade on the National Stock Exchange
by 13.5 million individual investors, each tagged with a postal code. The authors
assign villages to postal codes within five kilometers, keep the 4,154 postal codes
that received their first program road between October 2004 and February 2015, and
estimate a monthly panel with postal-code, month, and district-by-year fixed effects.
Every unit is eventually treated, so the comparison is only ever about timing
(@sec-causal-did discusses what that costs). A new outcome on an accepted design is a
legitimate contribution, and it leaves the referee's attention for the mechanism
sections, which is where this paper wants it.

**The main effect is split once before any mechanism is discussed.** New investors,
defined as accounts less than three years old, drive most of the response. In the 2022
draft the effect is about six additional new investors and 214 additional trades per
postal code per month, in a sample where the average postal code has 36 active
investors. Effects are larger in rural postal codes and in areas of intermediate
development. The poorest tenth by consumption shows no extra response relative to
developed areas. That split is a boundary result and a first hint about mechanism. It
is what one would expect if a road cannot create investors where there is little to
invest.

**Each route is written as a prediction about something other than the headline
outcome.** @fig-sw-roads-routes and @tbl-sw-roads-routes give the structure. The
information route says a road lowers the cost of learning about stocks, through
better access to facts about companies and through more contact with people who
already invest [@hong2004social]. If so, three things should follow, and none of them
is the participation count. Remote places, where information was scarcest, should
respond more. Portfolios should broaden. Holdings should reach toward firms farther
away. The financial-inclusion route says a road brings bank branches, and a branch is
where an account gets opened and where savings sit before they move. If so, the
effect should concentrate in postal codes where a branch opened after the road, and
money should leave savings deposits and consumption. A third candidate is a rival
more than a route: roads raise incomes, and richer households buy stocks. If that
were the whole story, the response should concentrate in months of good rainfall,
the standard proxy for a positive income shock in rural India.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-sw-roads-routes
%%| fig-cap: "The argument structure of the road-construction paper, reconstructed from the February 2022 working paper. Each route from road to participation is tested on an implication other than the participation count, and a final stage asks whether the new participants did well."
flowchart LR
  R["New feeder road<br/>(timing varies by<br/>postal code)"] --> I["Information route"]
  R --> F["Financial-inclusion<br/>route"]
  R --> W["Income shock<br/>(rival account)"]
  I --> I1["Larger where remote<br/>More tickers held<br/>More distant firms"]
  F --> F1["Larger where a branch<br/>follows the road<br/>Deposits and<br/>consumption fall"]
  W --> W1["Larger after good<br/>rainfall? No"]
  I1 --> P["More new investors<br/>and trades"]
  F1 --> P
  W1 -.-> P
  P --> Q["Did they do well?<br/>Short-run gains,<br/>long-run losses,<br/>more volatile stocks"]
```

| Route | Implication tested | Data brought in | Result in the 2022 draft |
|---|---|---|---|
| Information | Larger response in remote postal codes | Distance to the nearest large city (2011 Census) | New investors rise about 0.4% more per additional 10 km |
| Information | Broader portfolios | Count of distinct tickers traded | Up 51.1% |
| Information | Reach toward distant firms | Headquarters locations from a firm database | No increase for firms within 50 km; up 60.6% for firms more than 500 km away |
| Financial inclusion | Larger response where a branch opens within 36 months | Central bank register of branch openings | New investors up a further 8.9%, their trades 9.6% |
| Financial inclusion | Demand, not bank salesmanship | Branch ownership (state-owned or private) | Stronger for state-owned branches |
| Financial inclusion | Money moves out of savings and consumption | Branch-level deposit returns; a household panel in 16 districts | Savings deposits fall; consumption falls while income rises |
| Income shock (rival) | Response concentrated after good rainfall | Gridded monthly rainfall | Interaction not positive; negative for new investors |

: Routes from road to stock market participation, the implication each was tested on, and the data each test required. Results are from the February 2022 working paper. {#tbl-sw-roads-routes}

**Every route costs a new dataset.** The right-hand columns of @tbl-sw-roads-routes
list a census, a firm database, a confidential branch register, deposit returns, a
household survey, and a rainfall archive. Mechanism sections in student drafts
usually re-cut the main regression by variables already in the file. Here each claim
about a route is checked against a measurement that the main result did not use,
which is why seven rows read as seven pieces of evidence and not one result shown
seven ways.

**The best split is the one on which two stories disagree.** A branch could raise
participation because households want to invest and now can, or because bank staff
sell investments. The authors argue that state-owned banks reach further into rural
areas but earn less fee income, and so have less reason to push stock trading. The
demand story therefore predicts a stronger effect for state-owned branches, and the
sales story a weaker one. The estimate is stronger for state-owned branches. This is
the move the third specimen reached toward: a moderator chosen because rival accounts
predict opposite signs. The published abstract adds a route the 2022 draft lacks,
risk sharing, under which roads should matter more where incomes are volatile, and
reports limited evidence for it. A route that was proposed, tested, and found weak
is reported as such, and it makes the two surviving routes more credible.

**The last stage qualifies the headline.** Participation is usually treated as a
good outcome, and the paper could have stopped there. It asks instead how the new
investors did. In the 2022 draft, trades after road completion earn money over 1-day
and 10-day holding periods, show no detectable profit over 25 days, and lose money
over 140 trading days, and trading shifts toward more volatile stocks. The published abstract keeps
the conclusion: infrastructure raises participation but not necessarily the quality
of investment outcomes. This is a fourth stage beyond effect, mechanism, and
boundary, and it changes the policy sentence. Without it the paper recommends roads
as financial-inclusion policy. With it the paper says roads bring people in and
something else has to help them invest well.

**Where the specimen is thin.** The honesty requirement of @sec-sw-emb applies, and a
conference discussion of the working paper states the problem compactly
[@hong2022roaddiscussion]. A road moves everything at once: information, bank access,
and income. If bank branches were treated as the variable of interest and the road as
its instrument, the exclusion restriction would fail, because the road also works
through the other routes. The branch split has a second weakness. A branch that opens
after the road is itself an outcome of the road, and banks choose where to open, so
the postal codes with new branches may be the ones where demand for investing was
about to rise anyway. The discussion asks which way causation runs between branches
and participation. The rainfall test addresses transitory income only, and a
permanent rise in income from better market access remains a live alternative. The
evidence supports "both routes are operating" and does not support a share for each.
A paper that needs shares has to write down a model, as in @sec-sw-measure-model, or
find separate variation in each route. The same discussion suggests a different
frame, the unplanned benefits of public-goods spending, which shows that the frame
was a choice.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Explaining one effect through several routes

1. Before any mechanism test, split the main effect on the margin that matters (here,
   new against experienced investors) so the reader knows whose behavior needs
   explaining.
2. Write each route as a causal sentence, then derive an implication for a variable
   other than the headline outcome.
3. Bring a new measurement to each implication. Re-cutting the main regression by
   variables already in the file is weaker evidence.
4. Include the dull rival (people simply got richer) and give it a test of its own.
5. Look for one split on which two versions of a route predict opposite signs.
6. Report a route that found little support. It makes the others more credible.
7. Say that the tests show which routes operate and do not apportion the effect among
   them, and flag any split that conditions on something the treatment itself caused.
8. End by asking whether the outcome you raised was good for the people concerned, and
   let the answer change the policy sentence.
:::

The template carries over to marketing questions where a distant cause is suspected of
moving a consumer outcome: broadband rollout and online shopping, a new store format
and category entry, a payment technology and spending. In each, the main effect is
the short part of the paper, and the list of routes, with one outside dataset apiece,
is the plan for the rest.

For the first of these, @sec-causal-iv-broadband lists published broadband studies by
outcome and by source of variation, which is a quick way to see which routes have
already been tested.


## The Lifecycle Paper: How Response Changes Across Stages {#sec-sw-lifecycle}

Many marketing questions are really about a process. A product is announced,
launched, reviewed, discounted, and retired. An event is advertised, held, and then
sold as a recording. A customer searches, buys, uses, and complains. A lifecycle paper
takes one response parameter, such as a price elasticity, an advertising effect, or
the weight of word of mouth, and asks how it changes from stage to stage. The finding
is the profile across stages, not a single number. Done well, the paper also says why
the profile has that shape. The two usual reasons are that different people act at
different stages, and that the same people know or want different things at different
stages. Separating them is the core analytical task of the genre.

The genre borrows from its neighbors. Each stage needs a credible estimate, as in
@sec-sw-emb. The gap between stages is decomposed into selection and within-person
change, as in @sec-sw-decomposition. The mechanism is often tested by moderation, as
in @sec-sw-emb-listings. What sets it apart is the axis everything is organized on:
a sequence of stages whose boundaries are fixed by an institution rather than by the
analyst.

**The specimen.** @cong2026livestream ask how demand for paid livestreams responds to
price before the stream and after it, when the recording is on sale
(@sec-price-lifecycle has the substance). On a Chinese knowledge-sharing platform,
2,299 talks sold at a price fixed for their whole life. Demand before the stream has
an elasticity of about $-1.2$, and demand for the recording about $-0.8$. The paper
traces the gap partly to who buys early (heavy users, who are more price-sensitive)
and partly to what buyers know (quality is uncertain until the ratings arrive), and
ends with stage-specific prices. The account below follows the authors' June 2026
arXiv version, which carries the published title.

| Section | What it contains | Rhetorical job |
|---|---|---|
| Introduction | Platforms market the run-up to a stream; recordings are an afterthought; three features of the setting; the two elasticities; the two mechanisms; the pricing number | Make the later stage a neglected object, and promise a clean comparison across stages |
| Literature | Livestreaming studies (all about the live stage); live versus taped content; advance selling | Show that each stream covers one stage or one kind of uncertainty, and that this paper spans the lifecycle |
| Context and data | A lifecycle figure (listing, stream, recording); price fixed after listing; promoted events dropped; 30-day windows covering 85% of sales | Define the stages by the institution, and say what stays constant across them |
| Identification and main results | One pooled model with a stage interaction; rich controls; coefficient-stability bound; double machine learning; similar-event-price instrument | Estimate the parameter in each stage, and test the gap formally |
| Mechanism 1: self-selection | Buyer activity by stage; elasticity by engagement group; the gap within each group | Measure how much of the gap is *who* buys |
| Mechanism 2: quality uncertainty | Review topics; smaller gaps for reputable creators, "hard" topics, and existing followers; buyers active in both stages | Show within-buyer change where theory says it should be large, and its absence where it should be small |
| Alternative explanations | Weekly elasticities flat within each stage with a jump at the stream; search costs acknowledged | Rule out that the stage boundary is an artifact of how the platform displays each stage |
| Policy | One price versus a price per stage; +2.3% revenue, more for unknown creators | Turn the gap into a decision, with the assumptions stated |
| Conclusion | Rebalance marketing toward the recording; one platform, learning content, no viewing data | Redeem the opening promise and bound how far it travels |

: Anatomy of a lifecycle paper, read from @cong2026livestream (arXiv version of June 2026). {#tbl-sw-lifecycle-anatomy}

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-sw-lifecycle-spine
%%| fig-cap: "The spine of a lifecycle paper. Stages are fixed by an institutional event, the parameter is estimated in each, and the gap between stages is split into a selection part and a within-buyer part before it is turned into a stage-specific policy."
flowchart LR
  S["Stages fixed by<br/>an event that changes<br/>information or buyers"] --> E["Parameter in<br/>each stage,<br/>one pooled model"]
  E --> G["Gap between<br/>stages, with a<br/>standard error"]
  G --> C["Selection:<br/>who acts in<br/>each stage"]
  G --> W["Within change:<br/>what the same buyers<br/>know or want"]
  C --> A["Rule out artifacts<br/>of how each stage<br/>is displayed"]
  W --> A
  A --> P["Stage-specific<br/>policy, with its<br/>assumptions stated"]
```

### The moves worth copying

**Let the institution define the stages.** The stages here are set by the platform:
the listing date, the stream, and the switch to recording. The analyst did not choose
them after looking at the data. The paper's first figure is the lifecycle itself, and
the data section says what stays constant across stages. The price cannot change
after listing, which is what makes a comparison of elasticities across stages
meaningful. Events the platform discounted partway through are dropped for the same
reason. The outcome windows (30 days on each side) are set so that stages are
comparable across events, and the paper reports that they capture 85% of sales, so a
reader can judge what was left out.

**Test the gap, not two separate estimates.** The main specification pools both stages
and interacts price with a post-stream indicator, so the difference in elasticities
has its own standard error. Separate regressions for each stage appear only as a
robustness check. The authors justify this in a footnote, and it is worth copying.
Note also what the pooled form buys for identification. If an omitted creator
quality shifts demand equally in both stages, it biases the two elasticities by the
same amount and leaves the gap unbiased. Saying this out loud tells a referee which
claim is the robust one.

**Describe who acts in each stage before modeling why.** The first mechanism table is
plain description: buyers before the stream have written more answers and have more
followers than buyers of the recording. Only then does the paper estimate
elasticities by buyer type. The order matters, because a selection story that has not
first been shown in the raw composition reads as speculation.

**Split the gap into selection and within-buyer change.** The two explanations make
different predictions. If the gap is pure selection, it vanishes once buyer type is
held fixed. If buyers' information changes, the gap survives within type. The paper
runs this test twice: within engagement groups, and on the buyers who purchased in
both stages, a group that holds composition fixed by construction. The gap survives
both. A coarse proxy for type leaves some selection inside each group, so the
within-type gap is an upper bound on within-buyer change. The simulation below shows
why the test works.

```{r sw-lifecycle-selection}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
set.seed(2026)
J  <- 2000                                  # events, each sold before and after the stream
lp <- rnorm(J, log(20), 0.6)                # log price (RMB); fixed for the event's whole life
xi <- rnorm(J, 0, 0.5)                      # event appeal, independent of price here
eta <- c(frequent = 1.6, infrequent = 0.6)  # each type's price sensitivity

# Demand for event j in stage s from consumer type k is Poisson with mean
#   scale * share(k, s) * exp(xi_j - eta_ks * (lp_j - log 20)),
# where eta_ks = eta_k + shift if s is the pre-event stage (quality still uncertain).
simulate <- function(freq_pre, freq_post, shift_pre) {
  grid <- expand.grid(j = 1:J, stage = c("pre", "post"), type = names(eta),
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  share <- ifelse(grid$type == "frequent",
                  ifelse(grid$stage == "pre", freq_pre, freq_post),
                  ifelse(grid$stage == "pre", 1 - freq_pre, 1 - freq_post))
  e <- eta[grid$type] + ifelse(grid$stage == "pre", shift_pre, 0)
  grid$lp <- lp[grid$j]
  grid$q  <- rpois(nrow(grid), 400 * share * exp(xi[grid$j] - e * (grid$lp - log(20))))
  grid
}

# Elasticity in each stage from log(1 + demand) on log price, as in a stage-interacted model.
stage_elasticities <- function(d) {
  d$post <- as.integer(d$stage == "post")
  b <- coef(lm(log1p(q) ~ post * lp, data = d))
  c(pre = unname(b["lp"]), post = unname(b["lp"] + b["post:lp"]))
}
summarise <- function(d) {
  agg <- aggregate(q ~ j + stage + lp, data = d, FUN = sum)   # what the platform sees
  pooled <- stage_elasticities(agg)
  within <- sapply(names(eta), function(k) unname(diff(stage_elasticities(d[d$type == k, ]))))
  round(c(pre = pooled[["pre"]], post = pooled[["post"]],
          gap = pooled[["post"]] - pooled[["pre"]],
          gap_within_frequent = within[["frequent"]],
          gap_within_infrequent = within[["infrequent"]]), 2)
}

scenarios <- list(
  "Selection only"   = c(freq_pre = 0.8, freq_post = 0.2, shift_pre = 0),
  "Uncertainty only" = c(freq_pre = 0.5, freq_post = 0.5, shift_pre = 0.4),
  "Both"             = c(freq_pre = 0.8, freq_post = 0.2, shift_pre = 0.4)
)
res <- t(sapply(scenarios, function(p) summarise(do.call(simulate, as.list(p)))))
knitr::kable(res, col.names = c("Pre elasticity", "Post elasticity", "Gap (post - pre)",
                                "Gap within frequent", "Gap within infrequent"))
```

In the first row, no buyer's price sensitivity changes at all. Frequent, price-sensitive
users simply make up 80% of the early market and 20% of the late one. The aggregate
data still show demand that is far more elastic before the event (about $-1.4$) than
after it (about $-0.8$), close to the pattern in the paper. Only the split by type
gives it away: within each type the gap is zero. In the second row, the buyer mix is
constant and every buyer becomes less price-sensitive once quality is known, so the
gap appears both in aggregate and within each type. In the third row, both are at
work and the aggregate gap is roughly their sum, while the within-type gap recovers
the uncertainty part alone. This is the logic of the paper's Table 10. The aggregate
gap cannot tell the stories apart; the within-type gap can.

**Test the within mechanism by where it should be weak.** Quality uncertainty predicts
a smaller gap wherever buyers already knew what they were getting: creators with a
quality badge, "hard" topics whose quality can be judged from a description, and
buyers who already followed the creator. Each prediction is stated before its table,
and each holds. As in @sec-sw-emb-listings, moderation is consistent with the
mechanism without isolating it, and the paper concedes that live and recorded content
differ in other ways too.

**Check that the boundary is not an artifact of the display.** Platforms often show each
stage differently. Here upcoming events sit at the top of the page and past events
drift down it. If position drove the gap, elasticities would trend within each stage.
Instead they are flat on both sides with a jump at the stream. The paper says plainly
that it cannot rule out higher search costs for archived events. Naming the
alternative you cannot exclude costs less credibility than letting a referee name it.

**End with a policy and the assumption it rests on.** The counterfactual compares one
price for the whole life with a price for each stage, under linear demand and
independent stages. The authors call the second assumption "admittedly strong" and
name the dependence it ignores (cheap early tickets could cannibalize the recording
or signal quality to its buyers). A lifecycle counterfactual almost always rests on
some assumption about how stages are linked, so state it and say which way relaxing
it would move the answer.

**A lesson from the version history.** The first public version (arXiv, July 2021)
was titled "The Role of 'Live' in Livestreaming Markets." It estimated a daily
elasticity curve from two weeks before to two weeks after the stream with a
generalized orthogonal random forest. Elasticity was about $-0.5$ two weeks out,
near zero on the stream day, and about $-0.1$ afterward, and the paper attributed the
stream-day pattern to the chance to interact with the creator in real time. The
published paper (June 2026 arXiv) is plainer and stronger. The question became how
demand changes across the lifecycle rather than what "live" is worth. The daily curve
became a two-stage contrast with a pooled test and an instrument. The real-time
interaction mechanism was dropped, because weekly elasticities in the run-up to the
stream turned out to be flat. A self-selection mechanism and a pricing counterfactual
were added. Coarser stages identified cleanly made a better paper than a
fine-grained curve identified by a flexible method, and the mechanism the data no
longer supported was cut rather than kept.

**The genre in this book.** Many papers already cited here have the same shape, and
reading them as one genre makes the moves easier to see.

- @elberse2003 model movies released in sequence across countries, where performance
  in the first market shapes demand and screen allocation in later ones.
- @weinberg2000salesthrough treat theatrical release and video as sequential channels
  and ask when the second stage should open, given that it cannibalizes the first.
- @moe2002 use advance purchase orders, the pre-release stage, to forecast sales after
  launch.
- @liu2006wordmouth trace movie word of mouth from before release through the run and
  ask which features of it predict box office at each point.
- @eliashberg2000 build a decision-support model for evaluating a movie before release.
- @golder2004 explain the turning points of the product life cycle (takeoff and
  slowdown) with informational cascades.
- @deighton2012addingbricks show that the effect of opening stores on a retailer's
  catalog and online channels changes with time since opening.
- @lemon2016 organize customer experience into pre-purchase, purchase, and
  post-purchase stages, the conceptual frame for journey papers.
- @colicev2019 link firm and user content to separate stages of the marketing funnel.
- @kim2026customization ask whether a first customization experience changes the later
  stages of a customer's journey, and separate who customizes from what customizing
  does with a randomized experience manipulation (@sec-causal-born-or-made).
- @xie2001advance give the theory for the stage before consumption, when buyers are
  uncertain about their own future state.

::: {.callout-tip}
## A checklist for writing your own lifecycle paper

1. Define the stages by an event that changes what buyers know or who is buying
   (announcement, release, first reviews, the event itself, expiry), not by calendar
   time. Draw the lifecycle as the paper's first figure.
2. State what is held constant across stages (price, product, display) and drop units
   where the firm intervened partway through.
3. Choose windows that make stages comparable across units, and report how much of
   total activity they capture.
4. Estimate one pooled model with stage interactions so the gap has a standard error,
   and keep separate per-stage regressions as robustness.
5. Identify the level of the parameter in every stage; then say which confounds the
   pooled form differences out of the gap.
6. Show who acts in each stage with descriptive tables before proposing any
   mechanism.
7. Split the gap into selection and within-buyer change: estimate by buyer type, and
   on buyers active in more than one stage. Report how much of the gap survives.
8. For each within-buyer mechanism, name the units where it should be weak, state the
   prediction before the table, and test it.
9. Check whether the stage boundary is an artifact of how the platform presents each
   stage: look for a jump at the boundary rather than a trend within stages.
10. Turn the gap into a stage-specific policy, write down the assumption that links the
    stages (cannibalization, signaling, strategic waiting), and say which way relaxing
    it would move the answer.
11. Bound the claim: one platform, one kind of content, one period.
:::


## The Field-Experiment Paper from an Emerging Market {#sec-sw-emerging-field}

A growing share of the data that marketing students hold comes from markets the
field's journals rarely see: a panel of retailers in Vietnam, a survey of vendors in
Lagos, transaction logs from a network of mobile-money agents. Writing a paper from
such data runs into a problem that none of the templates above solves on its own.
The paper usually offers no new theory and no new method. Its evidence does not come
as a list of hypotheses, each confirmed by a coefficient. What it has instead is a
setting where an important question can be answered cleanly, and a design that
answers it. Turning that into a paper takes craft. @anderson2026datadecisions,
published online in *Marketing Science* in October 2026, is a well-built specimen. It
is a close cousin of the effect–mechanism–boundary paper (@sec-sw-emb): a randomized
experiment supplies the effect, and measured intermediate outcomes carry the
mechanism.

(The published article was not accessible when this section was written. The
publisher deposits a one-sentence abstract with Crossref. The fuller sources are the
abstract of a 2022 working paper in the Private Enterprise Development in Low-Income
Countries (PEDL) series, the abstract of a 2023 SSRN version, the trial's entry in the
AEA RCT Registry (AEARCTR-0005591), the article's deposited reference list, and Chicago
Booth Review coverage, including a 2024 article and a 2026 podcast interview with
Chintagunta [@chicagobooth2024apps; @chicagobooth2026podcast]. Each number below names the version it comes from. Where versions
disagree, the text says so. The section structure discussed here is a reconstruction
of what a paper in this genre must contain, not the article's table of contents.)

### The study in two paragraphs

The authors randomized 550 growth-oriented micro and small enterprises in Rwanda into
three arms (registry). Two hundred fifty treatment firms received an Android
smartphone, a data plan, and MARKETmanager, an app the researchers designed. Owners
used it to record sales, products, customers, and marketing actions, and it returned
monthly reports comparing the firm's current performance with its past. Fifty placebo
firms received the phone and data plan without the app. Two hundred fifty control
firms received nothing during the study and were promised access afterward. The
registry dates the intervention from July 2019 to March 2020. The 2022 working paper
describes nine months of treatment, and the 2024 Booth Review article seven, ending
as COVID-19 arrived. Staff visited treated owners to help them enter and read the
data: weekly according to the registry, monthly according to the 2024 article. That
article adds that the visitors explained the reports but gave no advice on what to do
with them. In the podcast, Chintagunta describes the visitors as mostly undergraduates
chosen for their lack of business experience.

The findings come in four families, listed in the same order in every version of the
abstract. Usage started low and rose by the third month. The 2022 abstract reports
daily usage rates of 90–95%. The 2024 article reports that about 30% of treated firms
used the app daily at first, rising to 60%. The two figures probably measure different
things, and only the paper can settle which. On mental performance, "objective
ability and psychological tests" (six of them, according to the 2024 article) show
gains in reasoning, memory, logic, and calculation. On practices, treated firms
adopted product-management activities, with spillovers into accounting practices the
app never targeted. On money, monthly sales were 36.4% and monthly profits 29.2%
higher than in the control group on average. These two figures appear in the 2022,
2023, and published abstracts. The published abstract adds that comparisons with the
placebo arm, which holds phone and internet access fixed, attribute the gains to the
analytics rather than the device.

### Where the contribution comes from without a new theory or method

A paper like this does not claim to have invented anything. Its contribution is one,
or several, of three other kinds, and the specimen makes all three.

1. *A causal estimate of a quantity people already act on.* Governments, donors, and
   software vendors already sell analytics to small firms on the assumption that it
   pays. The gap is not a missing theory but a missing number. The 2023 abstract says
   so in one line: analytics is "widely promoted", but evidence on its effects for
   individual entrepreneurs "remains limited". An evidence gap of this kind is
   legitimate when the quantity is policy-relevant and nobody has randomized it.
2. *A mechanism measured, not asserted.* "Analytics improves decisions" is usually an
   assumption. Here it becomes an observation, because the authors tested the owners
   themselves. A battery of cognitive tests is a measurement contribution in a
   marketing journal, and it turns a firm-level result into a claim about people.
3. *A tension resolved.* The 2022 abstract opens with two literatures that predict
   opposite signs. In one, technology builds the user's human capital. In the other,
   analysis paralysis, confirmation bias, information overload, and "brain drain"
   erode it. The deposited reference list covers both: studies of cognitive training
   and neuroplasticity on one side, and on the other a 2025 experiment in which
   generative AI without guardrails harmed high-school students' learning. A
   two-sided prior is what makes an empirical answer a contribution
   (@sec-sw-open-question). Neither side could have called the result in advance.

The contribution sentence of @sec-sw-contribution adapts accordingly. It becomes:
"We estimate the effect of [a treatment decision makers already buy or fund] on [the
outcomes they care about] among [a population described by its economic role], a
quantity prior work could not estimate because [the treatment is everywhere where data
are rich, or nobody randomized it], and we show that the effect runs through
[measured intermediate outcomes]."

The title history shows the same move. The 2022 working paper asked a question: "Is
(Smart) Technology Really Making Us Dumber?" The 2023 SSRN version answered it:
"(Smart) Technology Doesn't Make Us Dumber". The published title drops the
provocation altogether: "From Data to Decisions: Marketing Analytics, Mental
Performance, and Firm Growth in an Emerging Market". It names the causal chain in
order and puts the setting last, as a scope condition. The country does not appear in
it at all.

### The country as the source of variation, not a curiosity

The hardest sentence in an emerging-market paper answers the question a referee in
Chicago or Rotterdam is silently asking: why should I care about Rwanda? The weak
answer describes the country. The strong answer says what the country makes
estimable. In rich markets almost every firm already has some data, so the value of
analytics cannot be estimated from a starting point of none. In the specimen's
setting, few micro and small enterprises "formally record their marketing data"
(registry). In the podcast, Chintagunta puts the baseline share with any records at
about 30%. The setting is where the treatment can be switched on from zero. Write the
setting paragraph as an argument about variation, and the reader stops treating the
country as exotic.

The second move puts the reader's own literature beside the result.
@bargill2024ebay randomized eBay's Seller Hub, a data-rich seller dashboard, and found
that access raised sellers' revenues by 3.6% on average. The same question in a rich
platform setting produced an effect about a tenth the size. The outcomes, populations,
and measurement all differ, so the comparison is a hypothesis about where analytics
pays most, not an estimate. Stated that way, it gives a US reader a reason to care:
your number is small because your firms already know what this treatment teaches.

The third move describes the firms by their economic role, not their geography. Most
are retail shops, with some services such as hair salons (podcast). The registry
frames them as the last mile through which large companies reach consumers in
emerging markets. A brand manager at a consumer-goods firm recognizes that population
at once.

The fourth move is a research program. The same team has varied the marketing lever
while holding the population type fixed. Marketing versus finance training came first
in South Africa [@anderson2018], then volunteer marketers in Uganda
[@anderson2021marketersmatter], customer-feedback seeking in Rwanda
[@kaul2025callmemaybe], and now analytics. The Uganda paper appeared in the *Journal
of Marketing* issue on better marketing for a better world, whose editorial invites
work of this kind [@chandy2021better]. Each paper inherits the credibility of the last
one's fieldwork. A student with one emerging-market dataset should ask early which
second paper the same population and instruments could support.

Two habits of style follow. Name the country in the setting section, not in the
headline claim. And give the real reason for the choice of country alongside the
scientific one. Chintagunta says plainly in the podcast that the study went to Rwanda
partly because the research funding was there. Chintagunta also cites the country's push on
technology access and its heavy use of mobile payments. A paper can state both. It
should not claim the country was picked for representativeness unless it was.

### Evidence without hypothesis tests: the design is the argument

The specimen has no H1 through H4. In their place it has a design whose arms define
the estimands, and outcome families reported in causal order. The table below
reconstructs the estimands from the registry's design.

| Contrast | What it estimates | What a writer must say about it |
|---|---|---|
| Treatment vs. control | The whole bundle: phone, data, app, and support visits | This is the policy-relevant effect of offering the program |
| Treatment vs. placebo | The app and its support, holding phone and internet fixed | It answers "it's just the smartphone", but the placebo arm has only 50 firms, so the contrast is less precise |
| Placebo vs. control | Phone and data alone | A useful null if it is small, and a finding in its own right if not |

: The estimands implied by a three-arm design with a placebo, reconstructed from the registry entry for @anderson2026datadecisions. {#tbl-sw-emerging-estimands}

Several practices then replace hypothesis-by-hypothesis testing.

- *Report outcome families in causal order.* Usage, then mind, then practices, then
  money. Each family is reported as an effect with a confidence interval, not as a
  verdict on a hypothesis. The order is the story: a reader who has seen take-up and
  cognition is ready to believe the sales figure.
- *Separate the offer from the use.* With usage low at first, the intent-to-treat
  effect answers the policy question of what offering the app does. Scaling by usage
  (treatment on the treated) answers how much using it does. Report both, and say which
  one the abstract quotes. The public versions do not say which estimate the 36.4%
  is.
- *Be exact about registration.* The trial was registered on March 24, 2020, after the
  intervention began in July 2019, and no analysis plan appears on the public page. A
  writer in that position should say "registered" and not "pre-registered", should
  name the primary outcomes (here sales and profits), and should label everything else
  as secondary or exploratory. Readers forgive late registration far more readily than
  a claim that turns out to be false.
- *Control multiplicity by family.* Six cognitive tests and a list of practice items
  invite fishing. The standard remedy is a summary index per family, with p-values
  adjusted across families [@anderson2008multiple]. That paper is in the specimen's
  reference list, which suggests, though the public versions cannot confirm it, that
  the authors use this approach.
- *Show the mechanism through intermediate outcomes, and say what that cannot prove.*
  The reference list includes the causal-mediation framework of @imai2010general.
  Cognition and practices were not themselves randomized, so a mediation estimate
  rests on sequential ignorability (@sec-causal-mediation-assumptions). The safe claim
  is that the effect on intermediate outcomes and the effect on profits line up as
  the mechanism predicts. The placebo arm strengthens that claim, but it cannot turn
  it into an experiment on the mediator.
- *Treat heterogeneity as a test of mechanism, not a search.* The reference list
  includes generalized random forests, debiased machine learning for conditional
  average treatment effects, and lasso-based selection of controls, the current
  toolkit for heterogeneity in experiments. Use the forest for discovery and label it
  that way. Separately, name two or three subgroups that the mechanism says should
  gain more, such as owners with weak baseline numeracy if the mechanism runs through
  calculation skill. In the podcast, Chintagunta says that the owners who already kept
  records showed directionally similar gains but were too few to test. Writing that
  sentence is the honest version of a heterogeneity result.
- *Benchmark the magnitude.* A 29.2% profit gain means little until it is compared
  with something. The 2024 Booth Review article reports the authors' cost
  calculation: about \$4–\$6 a month in variable cost, an unsubsidized up-front cost
  of \$170–\$210 per business, and break-even in roughly 7–10 months. Set that
  against the alternatives a funder would consider. The same team's volunteer
  marketers raised monthly profits by 35.8% in Uganda [@anderson2021marketersmatter].
  Classroom training has a mixed record, which @mckenzie2021training reassesses.
  Intensive consulting worked for large Indian textile plants but at a much higher
  cost per firm [@bloom2013management]. Express the effect as a percentage of the
  control mean, in local currency and in dollars at a stated exchange rate, and per
  dollar spent.

### The institutional section as persuasion

In a paper from an unfamiliar market, the setting and intervention sections do work
that a literature review does elsewhere. They make the reader trust a design they
cannot picture. Four kinds of detail carry most of the weight.

- *Who the firms are.* Sector mix, size, how they were recruited, what "growth-oriented"
  meant as a screening rule, and how the sample compares with a national benchmark.
  The specimen's reference list includes Rwanda's 2020 Establishment Census, the
  natural benchmark for that comparison.
- *What the treatment was, screen by screen.* What owners entered and how often,
  what came back, and what the visitors were and were not allowed to say. The podcast
  gives the level of detail a reader needs. Owners entered whether the shop was open
  and its revenue each day. Every two weeks they entered their top three products
  with price and cost, from which the app computed margins, together with counts of
  regular, occasional, and new customers. Detail of this kind is persuasive because it
  rules out the most damaging alternative, that the program was really free
  consulting. Visitors chosen for their lack of business experience serve the same
  purpose.
- *What everyone else received.* Placebo firms had their data plans topped up, and
  every arm had enumerator visits (podcast). Balanced contact is the main answer to
  Hawthorne effects and experimenter demand, and it belongs in the design section, not
  in a footnote.
- *How the design changed.* An earlier PEDL-funded project by the same team, active
  2016–2018, describes a larger plan on its public page: 1,500 owners around Kigali, a
  finance-information tool and a marketing-information tool in separate arms, and
  follow-ups at 12 and 18–24 months. The public record does not say whether the
  executed study is a revision of that plan. A referee who finds such a page will ask.
  One paragraph explaining what changed and why pre-empts the question.

### Would it work elsewhere?

The external-validity paragraph is where emerging-market papers most often say too
much or too little. The productive form names the conditions under which the effect
should travel, not a list of countries. For the specimen those conditions are
plausibly three: owners do not already track their key numbers, the owner makes the
decisions, and the phone and data cost little relative to monthly profit. Each
condition can be checked against another market's data. Chintagunta declines to
extrapolate to US corner stores, saying such a claim would be "anecdotal" (podcast).
That restraint is a model to copy. Two further caveats belong in the paragraph. The
sample was screened for growth orientation, so the estimate describes firms that pass
that screen, not the median microenterprise. And persistence is a separate question.
The 2024 article reports a March 2021 follow-up of 14 randomly chosen treated owners,
13 of whom still kept records. Evidence that thin is useful as illustration and
should be labeled as such, not counted as a long-run estimate.

### Credible numbers where firms keep no books

The specimen's measurement problem is general to the genre, and in one respect it is
sharper. The published abstract says treated firms "report" higher sales and profits,
and the verb matters: in settings without books, outcomes are self-reported. Here the
treatment is record-keeping, so it changes the instrument that measures the outcome.
Treated owners may report more accurately, or more optimistically, than control owners
who are guessing. The defenses a referee will look for are these:

1. Measure outcomes with the same enumerator protocol in every arm. Never use the
   app's own records as the outcome for treated firms, because control firms have no
   such records.
2. Collect several follow-up rounds and average them. Noisy outcomes like
   microenterprise profits gain more power from repeated measurement than from extra
   firms [@mckenzie2012moret], a paper the specimen cites.
3. Cross-check reported profit against reported sales minus reported costs, and state
   the trimming or winsorizing rule before looking at treatment effects.
4. Pair self-reports with outcomes that are hard to inflate. Business practices
   measured as a standard index of yes/no items [@mckenzie2017practices] and objective
   cognitive tests both qualify. In the podcast, Chintagunta describes the Cognitive
   Reflection Test [@frederick2005crt], with about 0.7 of three items correct in the
   control group against about one in the treatment group. These are oral,
   approximate figures. The exact estimates are in the paper.
5. Ask whether a test measures the trained skill or general ability. An owner who
   computes margins every two weeks has practiced arithmetic. A gain on a calculation
   test is near transfer. A gain on reasoning or memory tests is the more surprising
   claim and needs the stronger defense. The specimen's reference list includes the
   cognitive-training literature in which this distinction is argued.
6. Report attrition by arm and bound the estimates for it. The public versions give no
   attrition figures. The study ended as COVID-19 arrived, which makes the timing of
   the endline survey and the response rate worth a paragraph of their own.
7. Account for local shocks. The reference list includes spatially robust standard
   errors and satellite night-lights data, which suggests the authors treat local
   economic conditions explicitly. That is worth doing whenever firms cluster in a
   few markets.

### The anatomy of the genre

| Section | Rhetorical job | What the specimen supplies (version) |
|---|---|---|
| Title | Name the causal chain; put the setting last, as scope | Data, decisions, mind, growth; "an emerging market" (published title) |
| Abstract | One number per outcome family, in causal order | Usage, cognition, practices, sales and profits (all abstracts) |
| Introduction: the tension | Show that the answer is not known in advance | Technology builds vs. erodes human capital (2022 abstract) |
| Introduction: the gap | Present a missing causal estimate, not a missing theory | Analytics widely promoted, evidence limited (2023 abstract) |
| Setting | Turn the country into the source of variation | Few firms record marketing data (registry); about 30% kept records (podcast) |
| Intervention | Make the treatment replicable and rule out "it was just advice" | Entry cadence, monthly reports, visitors who give no advice (registry; podcast; 2024 article) |
| Design | Let the arms define the estimands, with a placebo for the obvious objection | 250 treatment, 50 placebo, 250 control (registry) |
| Data and measurement | Show that outcomes are credible without books | Same contact for all arms; objective tests (podcast; abstracts) |
| Results: take-up | Show the first stage before any effect | Usage rises by month three (all abstracts) |
| Results: mind | Mechanism measured on the person | Reasoning, memory, logic, calculation (all abstracts) |
| Results: practices | Mechanism measured on the firm, including untargeted spillovers | Product management; accounting (all abstracts) |
| Results: money | The policy number | Sales +36.4%, profits +29.2% (2022, 2023, published abstracts) |
| Heterogeneity | Test the mechanism; label discovery as discovery | Forest and debiased-ML methods (reference list) |
| Cost and benchmarks | Make the magnitude interpretable | \$4–\$6 a month; break-even 7–10 months (2024 article) |
| Scope | Conditions under which the effect should travel | Restraint on extrapolating to the United States (podcast) |

: A reconstructed anatomy of the emerging-market field-experiment paper. The published article's own section structure was not accessible. The rows give the jobs a paper in this genre has to do, with the evidence for each in the public versions of @anderson2026datadecisions. {#tbl-sw-emerging-anatomy}

### When your own data were not randomized

Most students with emerging-market data have a survey, a panel, or a partner's
transaction logs, not an experiment. Most of the template still applies. The country
is still a source of variation, the institutional section still has to make a design
believable, the outcome families can still be ordered as a chain, and the measurement
defenses apply unchanged. What changes is the design paragraph. The arms that define
the estimands become an identification argument: a policy rollout, a boundary, or a
staggered adoption whose timing the firm did not choose. Those arguments are developed
in @sec-sw-emb-listings and @sec-causal-inference. If no such argument is available, the
honest genre is the descriptive paper (@sec-sw-descriptive), whose contribution is a
pattern that nobody had documented, stated with its own ceiling.

::: {.callout-tip}
## A checklist for writing your own emerging-market paper

1. Write the setting paragraph as an argument about variation: say what the country
   lets you estimate that a rich-data market cannot.
2. Put the closest result from a high-income setting beside yours, and explain the
   difference in magnitude as a hypothesis rather than a finding.
3. Describe the firms by their economic role (retailers, suppliers, agents) and
   benchmark the sample against a national census or survey.
4. State the contribution as an estimate, a measured mechanism, or a resolved tension,
   and name the decision maker who needs the number.
5. Let the arms or the identifying variation define the estimands, and include a
   placebo or comparison that answers the most obvious objection.
6. Report outcome families in causal order, one index per family, with multiplicity
   adjusted across families.
7. Give both the effect of the offer and the effect of use, and say which one the
   abstract quotes.
8. Say exactly when the study was registered and what was pre-specified.
9. Present mechanisms through intermediate outcomes, and state the assumption that a
   mediation estimate needs.
10. Name the subgroups the mechanism predicts before running exploratory
    heterogeneity, and report underpowered subgroups as underpowered.
11. Measure outcomes with one protocol across arms, average several rounds, and pair
    self-reports with measures that are hard to inflate.
12. Cost the intervention and compare it per dollar with the alternatives a funder
    would consider.
13. Write the external-validity paragraph as a list of conditions, and label thin
    follow-up evidence as illustration.
14. Give the real reason the study ran where it did, alongside the scientific one.
:::

## The Design-Science Method Paper {#sec-sw-design-science}

The methods paper sketched under paper types has a codified variant in information
systems that marketing scholars increasingly write for, review for, and borrow from:
the computational design-science paper. Its artifact is a method, usually a
predictive model, and its contribution is design knowledge, meaning a statement of
which design choices solve which problem and why
[@hevner2004design; @gregor2013positioning; @abbasi2024pathways]. Students who know
only the hypothesis-testing template find these papers hard to imitate, because the
logic that holds them together is never stated in any one place. The paper
reveals it through a handful of tables.

Two papers from the same September 2026 issue of *Information Systems Research* serve as
specimens. @wang2026drdl propose DRDL, a deep-learning method that predicts whether
and when a firm will fall into financial distress from several data sources at once
(@sec-mmf-drdl reimplements it). @xu2026upstar propose UPSTAR, a product recommender
that first infers *why* a customer bought each item, out of stable preference or
exploratory intent, and then predicts the next purchase. The domains share almost
nothing, but the architecture is the same, and the shared architecture is what to
learn. (DRDL was read in full. For UPSTAR, only the published abstract and the
authors' released code were accessible when this section was written, so statements
about UPSTAR's internals come from the code.)

### The spine: one artifact per challenge

The single most important object in a design-science paper is a table that most
readers skim: the design framework. It runs from goals to challenges to design
components, and it is built backward from the problem's own features. DRDL's version
(their Table 2) has two goals, five challenges, and five components, one component for
each challenge.

| Paper | Goal | Challenge | Design component |
|---|---|---|---|
| DRDL | Use entangled multiview data | Separate complementary from redundant signal | Discrete multiview recoder |
| | | Fuse views without carrying redundancy | Mask-based view fusion decoder |
| | Predict risk over several horizons | Risk must not fall as the horizon lengthens | Risk accumulation function |
| | | A firm that fails sooner must score riskier | Focal survival loss |
| | | The two objectives' gradients can conflict | Adaptive gradient balancing |
| UPSTAR (reconstructed) | Know why each item was bought | Motivation categories are left implicit | Framework of purchase motivations |
| | | Inferring motivation usually needs surveys or side data | STB measure from sequences and item attributes only |
| | Use motivation to predict the next purchase | The two motivations follow different dynamics | Separate sequence encoders, joined by a learned fusion gate |
| | | Exploratory signals are sparse and noisy | Teacher–student distillation from the motivation-specific heads |

: The design framework as the spine of a design-science paper. DRDL rows follow the authors' Table 2 [@wang2026drdl]; UPSTAR rows are reconstructed from the published abstract and the released code [@xu2026upstar], not from a table in the paper. {#tbl-sw-design-spine}

The table matters because every later section indexes into it. The method section has
one subsection per row. The ablation study removes the rows one at a time. The
comparison with related methods uses the challenges as its columns. The contribution
section restates the goals as design principles. Two failure modes are visible at
a glance. A component with no row is decoration, and a referee will ask why it is
there. A challenge with no component is a promise the paper never redeems.

Each goal usually comes with a kernel theory, a theory from outside the
method's field that explains why the design should work. DRDL draws on the
chunking theory of memory from cognitive psychology to justify discrete codes. UPSTAR
starts from a framework of purchase motivations and keeps the two that are rooted in
the consumer's own interests. The kernel theory is inspiration, not a hypothesis
under test, and the honest papers say so. DRDL calls it "a principled inspiration".
Referees judge it on whether the design traces back to it, not on whether the
experiments confirm it.

### The front half: question, gap table, rationale

The research questions are design questions, phrased as *how to*. DRDL's two are how to
