separate useful from redundant information across data views, and how to predict risk
over time while respecting two monotonicity constraints. The advice of
@sec-sw-open-question still applies, but differently: here the gap is a capability
gap, so it has to be shown, not asserted. DRDL shows it with a positioning table
of prior studies, with design properties as checkmark columns and "This study" as the
last row. The table note states the search rule: studies from 2020–2025 in the AIS
Senior Scholars' list of premier journals and in the Academic Journal Guide's operations
research and management science category (rated 3 and above), 57 candidates in all. That
note turns a literature review into an auditable claim. The table's columns
reuse the vocabulary of the design framework. So does a second table, which compares
the proposed method with the incumbent methods on the same property columns.

Between the literature and the method sits a section that hypothesis-testing papers
lack: methodological challenges and design rationale. It argues from the problem's
characteristics to each challenge, so that by the time the method appears, every
component already has a reason to exist.

### The method section

The method section follows a fixed order: a formal problem definition, an overview
figure, one subsection per component, and a subsection explaining why the design
should work (DRDL §4.7, "Mechanism of Disentanglement"). DRDL is also honest about
novelty, a habit worth copying. Its contribution paragraph separates the existing
building blocks it reuses, such as vector quantization and the multilayer perceptron,
from the five it designed. A referee who finds an uncredited standard component
discounts every other novelty claim in the paper.

### Evaluation at three levels

Both papers evaluate at three levels, and DRDL names them: model, application, and
mechanism.

**Model: does it predict better?** DRDL compares against 21 benchmarks from three
method families. Sixteen of them are four multitask architectures, each combined with
the monotonicity and ranking losses that earlier work proposed for the same two
properties. The baselines thus get the best existing fix for each challenge rather than
appearing as straw men. It runs five repetitions of 10-fold cross-validation for 50
estimates per cell, plus an out-of-time split. It reports ranking, horizon-specific,
and calibration metrics. Two appendices pre-empt the predictable objections. Gradient
boosting and parametric survival models on hand-built ratios answer "is the complexity
worth it?" Averaging and stacking ensembles answer "isn't this just an ensemble?" The
headline is a C-index of 0.775 against 0.712 for the best benchmark on yearly
Chinese-market prediction. UPSTAR's abstract reports gains over state-of-the-art
recommenders on three retail datasets.

**Application: is the gain worth anything?** Offline accuracy is not a decision, so
the paper translates it into the currency of the person who acts on it (the same rule
as item 8 above). DRDL simulates investment pools and counts the distressed firms each
method lets in, scores profitability by return on assets and equity, and repeats the
exercise under mean–variance weighting. For a recommender, the equivalent is what the
recommendations do for the retailer. UPSTAR's abstract stresses surfacing genuinely
exploratory items, which drive discovery and cross-category sales.

**Mechanism: why does it work?** "Mechanism" here means something different from
Stage 2 of @sec-sw-emb, and it stands on firmer ground. The author controls the artifact,
so removing a component is an intervention on the design rather than an inference from
observational data. Five kinds of evidence recur:

1. *Ablation tied to the spine.* Drop each component in turn. DRDL removes six,
   one at a time, and reports the performance gained per unit of training time for
   each. The mask-based fusion decoder delivers the most gain per second in both
   markets.
2. *Verify the property each component claims.* If a component claims to disentangle,
   measure disentanglement directly. DRDL scores its representations on two
   disentanglement metrics against two disentangled-VAE baselines. A component
   whose claimed property is never measured has only an ablation to its name, and an
   ablation cannot say *why* the drop happened.
3. *Locate the gain where the theory predicts it.* UPSTAR's headline mechanism
   evidence is that the improvement concentrates on exploration-driven purchases.
   That is where a motivation-aware design should help and a motivation-blind
   one should struggle.
4. *Rule out the cheap explanations:* more parameters, ensembling, class imbalance.
5. *Sensitivity and interpretability:* vary the hyperparameters the design introduced
   (codebook size in DRDL, the stable and exploratory cutoffs in UPSTAR), and show what
   the learned representations encode.

DRDL runs seven such analyses, most of them in online appendices. The main text
carries the ablation and the property check, because those two tie the evidence back
to the spine.

### Make the elaborate version beat the simple one

UPSTAR's released code shows why the simple version of your own idea should appear in
the paper. In the code, the paper's STB measure works like this. It builds an item
co-purchase graph and perturbs it adversarially. It then scores each item by how
little its learned embedding moves: robust items count as stable preference, fragile
ones as exploratory. Within each customer's history, the top half of items by score are
labelled stable and the bottom 40% exploratory. The repository's configuration offers
three STB variants. Its help text describes a repurchase-intensity score as "default &
best" and the original adversarial version as "degenerate". The repository ships
training code but no evaluation script. None of this shows that the published results
are wrong, and we have not rerun them. It does show the question a replicator will ask
first: does the sophisticated component earn its place over a one-line heuristic for
the same construct? The defense is to put that heuristic in the paper as a baseline and
beat it. The second defense is to release the code that regenerates the headline table,
not only the training loop.

### Carrying the template into a marketing journal

Design-science outlets judge the artifact. Marketing journals reading the same paper
weigh three further things.

- **Validity of any new measure.** A score like STB is a measurement claim: that a
  number computed from transaction logs tracks a psychological motivation. The
  standards of @sec-reliability-validity apply. That means convergent evidence against
  an external criterion, such as stated motivation or a known exploration episode, and
  discriminant evidence against confounds such as purchase frequency.
- **Decision value shown in the field.** An offline accuracy table persuades an IS
  referee more than a marketing one. A field experiment, or a credible policy
  counterfactual, carries the application level further.
- **The marketing question in front.** UPSTAR's motivation framework is the marketing
  hook. The architecture is the means. A marketing version of the paper leads with
  what the framework says about consumers and treats the recommender as the test of
  that framework.

::: {.callout-tip}
## A checklist for the design-science method paper

1. Phrase each research question as *how to design* something that achieves a stated
   property.
2. Build the design framework (@tbl-sw-design-spine) before drafting. Every component
   gets exactly one challenge, and every challenge gets a component.
3. Name the kernel theory, and present it as inspiration for the design, not a
   hypothesis the experiments test.
4. Back the gap claim with a positioning table whose selection rule sits in the table
   note, and reuse its property columns to compare against incumbent methods.
5. Separate reused building blocks from novel ones in the contribution statement.
6. Benchmark across method families, give strong baselines the best existing fix for
   each challenge, and report variance across repeated splits plus an out-of-time
   test.
7. Include the simple heuristic version of your own idea, and a tuned off-the-shelf
   learner on hand-built features, as baselines.
8. Translate accuracy into a decision outcome measured in the user's currency.
9. Ablate one component at a time, measure the property each component claims, and
   show the gain landing where the kernel theory predicts.
10. State the contribution as design principles, and release code that reproduces the
    headline table, not only the training loop.
:::

## The Interpretable Machine-Learning Paper: A Competitive-Intelligence Specimen {#sec-sw-interpretable-ml}

A second route from machine learning to a top-journal paper is quieter than the
design-science route. The paper builds no new architecture. It takes a well-understood
probabilistic model, extends it so that it can absorb data the original model never
saw, and arranges every estimated parameter so that it answers a question a manager
already asks. @qian2026competitive, published in *Production and Operations Management*,
is a clean specimen. They extend latent Dirichlet allocation to combine three traces
that users leave on a Chinese car platform (the cars they favorite, the cars whose
forums they comment in, and what they write there) and return a competitive map of
2,330 car models. @sec-tad-hlda covers the model and reimplements its core on simulated
data. This section reads the paper for its construction. (The full open-access article
was read; its online appendices were not.)

### The title states the managerial object first

The title follows a formula worth copying: *Deriving [a managerial object] from [a
data source]: an interpretable machine learning framework*. Competitive intelligence
is the object, user behavior data is the input, and the method comes last. An
operations or marketing editor sees a question their readers ask before they see an
algorithm. Compare a title that leads with the model's name. That title tells the
editor what was built but not why anyone should read it.

### Quantify the gap with a number anyone can check

Most methods papers assert that prior data are sparse. This one counts. Earlier
market-structure work inferred competition from products mentioned together in reviews
[@netzer2012]. The authors collected reviews from edmunds.com and autohome.com and found
that only 1.1% and 0.13% of them, respectively, mention more than one car. One sentence
turns a methodological complaint into a fact a referee can verify, and it motivates
the paper's whole design. If co-mentions are that rare, the information has to come
from somewhere else, and favorites and comment histories are where it is.

### The spine is a data-source table

In @sec-sw-design-science the spine runs from challenges to components. Here it runs
from data sources to roles (the paper's Table 1).

| Data source | What it reveals | Where it enters the model |
|---|---|---|
| Favorites lists | Serious consideration, close to purchase | Product embeddings learned from favorites, held fixed |
| Commented products | Broader attention, early in search | Topic-model documents; one mixture component draws on the embeddings |
| Comment text | Why products are compared | Word topics tied one-to-one to submarkets |

: The data-source spine of @qian2026competitive, after their Table 1. {#tbl-sw-hlda-spine}

Each row is justified by consumer behavior, not by the method. Favorites and comments
are said to capture different stages of the decision process, and the text explains
the comparison. The ablation study then removes rows from this table, one source at a
time. A reader who sees the table knows what the evaluation will test before reaching
it.

### Bound the novelty by naming the building blocks

The method section credits its parts. The base models are LDA [@blei2002lda] and
Correspondence LDA [@blei2003annotated], the two-component mixture comes from
@nguyen2015latentfeature, and the softmax over embeddings follows @dieng2020etm. The new
part is the composition: a mixture that lets favorites inform submarkets, a link that
makes the text conditional on them, and a joint sampler for both. That claim is
smaller than "a new model", and it is one a referee cannot take apart by finding the
pieces elsewhere.

### "Interpretable" means every estimand has a managerial name

The word *interpretable* in the title is a commitment. It does not mean that a black
box gets a post hoc explanation. The paper's section on competitive intelligence
(their §3.5) lists four quantities, each a posterior summary of a model parameter and
each named for a decision:

1. *Competitive strength* of a product in a submarket: the probability the submarket
   generates it, mixing comment co-occurrence and the favorites embedding.
2. *User perceptions* of a submarket: the word distribution of its linked topic, scored
   for sentiment.
3. *User preference* over submarkets: each user's mixture weights.
4. *Submarket popularity*: those weights averaged over users.

This mapping is the reason the paper can take an unsupervised model to an operations
journal. The reader never has to be told what a topic "means"; the model was built so
that each topic is a submarket and each topic weight is a share of attention.

### One focal firm carries the results

All the managerial results are told through one company, Tesla. The empirical section
finds Tesla's premium EV submarket and its neighbors, ranks the rivals in each, reads
the perception topics for each, and predicts where two new entrants will land (an NIO
sedan ranks seventh in Tesla's submarket, a BMW only seventeenth). A
single running case makes 60 submarkets readable and gives the managerial-implications
section something concrete to stand on.

### A validation stack, not a fit statistic

The paper presents four layers of evidence. Only the first is in the main text.

1. *Ablation by data source*: five variants, ten runs each, paired *t*-tests against
   the full model on topic coherence and perplexity.
2. *Parameter recovery*: simulate from the model with known parameters and check that
   the sampler recovers them.
3. *Benchmarks* against other topic and embedding models.
4. *External validation* against consumer reports, sales data, and human ratings of
   the submarkets.

The fourth layer is what turns a better-fitting model into a claim about markets.
Coherence and perplexity are both computed from the model's own outputs. A student
copying the template should treat external validation as required, not optional.

### Where the specimen is thin

A referee from a marketing journal would press on four points.

- **The gains are measured in fit, and they are small.** Against single-source
  variants, the full model improves coherence by about 5% and perplexity by about 4%.
  The variants that pair favorites with comments come within 3% on coherence. One
  ordering in the ablation also goes the other way. Adding text to comments without
  favorites makes both metrics *worse* than comments alone, so text helps only when
  the favorites embedding anchors the submarkets. The paper reads the ablation as
  showing that favorites are the most valuable source. It does not discuss why adding
  text alone lowers fit.
- **Strength is attention, not substitution.** A product's competitive strength is
  the share of a submarket's comment and favorites activity it attracts. The demand
  definition of a market is about who substitutes for whom
  [@desarbo2006competes; @ringel2016asymmetric]. Agreement with sales patterns, in an
  appendix, is consistent with substitution but does not establish it.
- **The number of submarkets was chosen by perplexity**, which tends to keep improving
  as topics are added, and the 60 submarkets are then read by hand.
- **The new-entrant forecast relies on vector arithmetic chosen by the analyst.** It
  approximates the Mercedes EQC as Audi e-tron − Audi Q7 + Mercedes GLC. The
  analogy is checked visually for one car. It is not tested on a set of launches
  whose later positions are known.

None of these is fatal. Each is a place where a revision would ask for one more table.
No code or data were released, which leaves the gains impossible to check from
outside.

### Carrying the template into a marketing journal

The acknowledgments show that the paper was handled in *POM* by marketing scholars, so
the genre already sits on the marketing–operations border. A version aimed at a
marketing journal would keep the spine and the named estimands and add three things.
It would validate submarkets against substitution measured from choice or
consideration data. It would add a held-out prediction test, for example the
following year's cross-shopping or the positions of cars launched after the training
window. And it would make one managerial decision visibly depend on the map.

::: {.callout-tip}
## A checklist for the interpretable machine-learning paper

1. Put the managerial object first in the title and the method last.
2. Quantify the data gap that motivates the method with a count a referee can
   reproduce.
3. Build the data-source table before drafting: each source gets a behavioral
   rationale and a place in the model.
4. Extend a model readers already trust, and name every borrowed building block.
5. Map every estimated parameter to a quantity with a managerial name, and define the
   mapping by equation.
6. Tell the results through one focal firm.
7. Ablate by data source with repeated runs and paired tests, and explain any ordering
   that contradicts the story.
8. Add parameter recovery on simulated data and external validation against outcomes
   the model never saw.
9. Include a prediction the incumbent methods cannot make, and test it on held-out
   cases rather than one illustration.
10. Release code and, where licensing allows, the processed data.
:::

## The Structural-Model Paper: A Consumer-Search Specimen {#sec-sw-structural}

A third paper from the same September 2026 issue of *Information Systems Research*
shows a different genre, the empirical structural-model paper. @zhang2026footprints model
how consumers search across a platform's native app and its mini-program, carrying a
reference price from one channel to the other, and use the estimates to design a
promotion (@sec-click-search-mss covers the substance). The artifact here is not a
method to be benchmarked, as in @sec-sw-design-science, nor a causal effect, as in
@sec-sw-emb. It is an *estimated model of behavior*, and the contribution is what the
model lets a decision maker do that a reduced-form analysis cannot. Structural papers
in marketing, economics, and IS share a skeleton, and this one shows it clearly.
(Only the two versions of the abstract and the deposited reference list were accessible
when this section was written, so what follows reads the paper's framing, not its
internals.)

### The title and the abstract

The title has two halves joined by a colon, a phenomenon and a model:
"Analyzing Consumer Footprints on E-Commerce Platforms: A Multichannel Sequential
Search Model with Reference Price." The first half echoes @ghose2019modeling, "Modeling
Consumer Footprints on Search Engines," and that echo positions the paper in an IS
tradition before the reader reaches the abstract. The second half lists the model's
ingredients in order of novelty: *multichannel* is new, *sequential search* is the
inherited framework, and *reference price* is the behavioral addition.

The Crossref abstract makes six moves in seven sentences, and each is one or two
sentences long:

1. **Context.** Mini-programs let consumers browse across the app and the mini-program,
   leaving click and purchase records in both.
2. **Opportunity.** These multichannel footprints contain information about search
   preferences that could improve multichannel management.
3. **Gap.** Prior studies focus on single-channel contexts that "may not directly apply."
4. **Model.** A threefold search across channels, products, and pages, with a
   reference price updated along the journey.
5. **Findings.** Heterogeneity in channel preferences, cross-channel costs, and
   reference-price sensitivity explains the variety of footprints.
6. **Policy.** A 32% average promotion gap between channels, and more profit from a
   smaller promotion than the state-of-the-art model achieves.

A second abstract, on the paper's record in City University of Hong Kong's
repository and marked "© 2026, INFORMS", swaps move 5 for a prediction claim ("significantly
outperforms the state-of-the-art sequential search models in predicting both clicks and
purchases") and quantifies move 6 as a 22% profit improvement. That pairing is the
genre's signature: the model is first shown to be *right* (it predicts held-out
behavior better than the incumbent model) and then shown to be *useful* (it changes a
decision, by an amount in money).

### The spine: data feature, model component, counterfactual lever

The design-science paper is held together by a table of challenges and components
(@tbl-sw-design-spine). The structural paper's equivalent links three things: a
*feature of the data* that the incumbent model cannot reproduce, the *model component*
added to reproduce it, and the *counterfactual lever* that the component makes
available. A component that changes no counterfactual is hard to justify; a lever with
no component behind it is a promise the paper cannot keep.

| Paper | Data feature | Model component | Counterfactual lever |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zhang et al. (2026) | Same products, two channels, different prices | Cross-channel search with channel-specific costs | Channel-specific promotion |
| | Prices seen early shape later clicks | Reference price updated along the journey | Promotion *gap* between channels |
| | Results arrive in pages | Cross-page search cost | (inherited from ranking work) |
| | Channels are linked by external links | Channel entry and switching costs | Aligning links with promotions |
| Hu & Karacaoglu (2024) | Mini-program sessions are longer and convert more | Fixed (entry) and marginal (per-click) search costs by channel | Referral credits on WeChat; coupons on the app |

: The structural paper's spine. Zhang et al. rows are reconstructed from the published abstracts; Hu & Karacaoglu rows follow their accepted manuscript [@hu2024westore]. {#tbl-sw-structural-spine}

The table also says where to spend pages. The paper has to show *model-free evidence*
for every data feature in the first column before the model appears (for example,
that consumers who saw a lower price in one channel click differently in the other),
because a referee who does not believe the feature will not believe the component.

### The sections, and what each must contain

A structural search paper usually runs in this order.

1. **Introduction**, ending with the policy number and a contribution paragraph for
   each literature the paper joins. This paper joins three, as its reference list
   shows: consumer search (Weitzman-type models from @weitzman1979optimal to
   @morozov2021estimation), reference prices (@mazumdar2005reference; @putler1992incorporating), and
   multichannel and mobile commerce. The contribution claim works because the three
   have rarely been combined. That is the "intersection" gap of @sec-sw-contribution, and
   it holds only if the intersection is really empty, which leads to the next item.
2. **Literature**, organized by stream, closing each stream with what this paper adds.
   The closest prior work deserves a paragraph of its own. The nearest predecessor here
   is @hu2024westore, a *Production and Operations Management* paper on the same app
   versus mini-program comparison, estimated on JD.com data with a sequential search
   model. It does not appear in the ISR paper's deposited reference list. Whether
   the two were developed in parallel we cannot tell. The lesson for authors is
   general: search the adjacent fields (operations, IS, economics) for the closest
   competitor, because a referee from that field will know it.
3. **Data and model-free evidence.** Sessions, channels, click order, prices, and
   purchases, with descriptive patterns tied to the spine's first column.
4. **Model.** Utility, search costs, the reference-price process, and the decision
   rules, stated as equations, with every departure from the canonical model flagged.
   A reference price that updates with prices seen during the search breaks one of
   Weitzman's independence assumptions. An honest paper says what the consumer is
   assumed to anticipate and what she is not.
5. **Identification.** Which variation in the data pins down which parameter: click
   order for preferences, stopping for search costs, cross-channel price differences for
   the reference-price parameters. The framework of @ursu2025sequential is now the
   standard reference for this argument.
6. **Estimation**: the simulator, its tuning, and a Monte Carlo study showing that the
   estimator recovers known parameters (@sec-click-search-sim does this for a stylized
   version).
7. **Results**: parameter estimates, heterogeneity, and fit against benchmark search
   models and machine-learning predictors (this paper's reference list includes a
   deep click-prediction model, xDeepFM).
8. **Counterfactuals.** The policy simulation, compared against the policy the
   benchmark model would have recommended. Choose counterfactuals the normalizations
   permit: price and promotion changes rather than search-cost changes.
9. **Robustness and conclusion.**

::: {.callout-tip}
## A checklist for the structural search paper

1. Make the title name the phenomenon first and the model second.
2. Build the spine (@tbl-sw-structural-spine) before drafting: every new component
   answers a data feature and opens a counterfactual lever.
3. Show model-free evidence for each data feature before the model.
4. Flag every departure from the canonical model, and say what it costs in optimality
   or identification.
5. Argue identification parameter by parameter, from the variation in the data.
6. Run a Monte Carlo recovery study for the estimator and report the tuning choices.
7. Beat the incumbent structural model *and* a flexible predictive model out of
   sample.
8. Run counterfactuals the normalizations allow, and compare against the incumbent
   model's recommendation.
9. Search adjacent fields for the closest prior paper and position against it
   explicitly.
:::

## The Observational Contagion Paper: A Fraud-Spread Specimen {#sec-sw-contagion-template}

Many marketing and finance questions are about spread: of word of mouth, of a product, of
a misconduct norm, of an investing habit. Usually there is no experiment and no clean
shock, only outcomes by place or person and a measured network. Papers in this genre
cannot claim identification in the strict sense, so their persuasiveness depends on
structure. @griffin2026fraud, on fraud in the U.S. Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), is a
well-built recent example from *The Review of Financial Studies*. The econometrics, with
our replication from the authors' package, are in @sec-graph-exposure. This section reads
the paper as a piece of writing.

### Title and abstract

The title is a yes-or-no question with a subtitle naming the setting: "Is Fraud
Contagious? Social Connections and the Looting of COVID Relief Programs." The question
repeats the title of @dimmock2018fraud, who asked it about coworkers at financial-advisory
firms. Reusing a known question tells finance readers which literature the paper extends
before they read a word of the abstract. The subtitle supplies the channel (social
connections) and a vivid object ("looting").

The abstract makes four moves in four sentences. It states a fact: fraud is
geographically concentrated. It states the main finding: high-fraud places are socially
linked, and fraud spreads over time along those links. It gives mechanism evidence:
members of fraud-promoting social media groups commit more fraud, and linked places use
the same FinTech lenders. It closes with policy: faster, data-driven detection and
prosecution. The abstract has no identification jargon. The identification argument
starts in the introduction.

### Rival hypotheses before the favored one

Section 1.2 sets out three hypotheses before any result. The first is an individualist
null: some people were more willing to commit fraud and took the chance. If so, local crime,
culture and demographics should explain where fraud happened, and social ties should add
nothing. The second is organized cybercrime using stolen identities, which predicts a link
to past identity theft. The third, social transmission, is grounded in Sutherland's
differential-association theory of crime: people learn both the techniques and the
rationalizations for an offense from their contacts.

The paper then gives the first two hypotheses a real test. Section 2 regresses fraud on
demographics, religious affiliation, public corruption, identity theft, suspicious-activity
reports and social capital, and it reports what works (identity theft, poverty, race) as
partial support for both. Only then does the social measure arrive, and it wins on
incremental $R^2$: it explains about ten times as much within-county variation as the
strongest demographic variable. Giving the favored hypothesis a fair fight against named
rivals is more persuasive than testing it alone. It also answers in advance the referee
who asks "isn't this just poverty?"

### The spine: one section per referee question

After the main estimate, every subsection heading in Section 3 is a question a skeptical
reader would ask, and each is answered by one exhibit.

| Section | Heading, as the reader's question | Worry it answers | Main exhibit |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 2 | Is fraud explained by demographics, corruption, crime? | Individual propensity | County and ZIP regressions |
| 3.1 | (Social proximity to suspicious lending) | Is the effect large? | Coefficients plus incremental $R^2$ |
| 3.2 | Concentrated in particular areas? | One subgroup drives it | Coefficient plot by median split |
| 3.3 | Do connections explain the spread over time? | Static correlation | Decile heat map; matched pairs; lagged regression |
| 3.4 | Driven by nearby regions? | Physical spillover | Binscatter; distance-restricted regressions |
| 3.5 | Homophily or omitted variables? | Reflection problem | Five numbered responses, ending in an Oster bound |
| 4 | Mechanisms | What actually travelled? | Social media groups; identical-loan clusters; lender choice |

: How @griffin2026fraud arranges its evidence. Headings paraphrased from the published paper. {#tbl-sw-contagion-spine}

Building this table before drafting is the most useful thing to take from the specimen.
List the worries a referee will raise, give each one a heading and an exhibit, and order
them from the most obvious alternative to the most subtle. Section 3.5 is the section
referees read most closely. The paper names the threat by its canonical source, Manski's
reflection problem [@manski1993reflection]. It concedes that the threat is hard to
eliminate. It then lists five numbered responses, each pointing back to evidence already
shown. Conceding the limit first makes the numbered responses easier to trust.

### Moves worth copying

- **Description first.** Figure 1 shows a county map, then within-county variation
  across ZIP codes, then fraud rates over time by lender type. The reader sees the
  variation to be explained before any model tries to explain it.
- **A network figure that makes an argument.** Figure 2 places ZIP codes of three
  cities on the sides of a triangle, sorted by fraud decile, with edge width showing
  tie strength. High-fraud nodes visibly connect to each other. Most network plots show
  only that a network exists. This one shows the result.
- **Magnitude in a portable unit.** All variables are standardized, so every coefficient
  reads in standard deviations, and the incremental-$R^2$ comparison gives a sentence
  readers remember ("ten times the next predictor").
- **Fingerprint outcomes as mechanism evidence.** The strongest section concerns outcomes
  that homophily cannot easily produce: clusters of loans identical in industry, amount
  and headcount, and the choice of a particular FinTech platform. A refrain recurs at the
  end of each mechanism test, that the pattern would be "difficult to explain if social
  connections merely proxy for homophily." Repeating one sentence ties the separate
  tests to a single claim.
- **Qualitative texture.** Group names and posts from fraud-promoting social media groups
  ("sauce", "methods"), and word clouds contrasting high- and low-fraud groups, make the
  mechanism concrete. The full posts go in an appendix exhibit. Differential-association
  theory explains why both techniques and rationalizations show up in them.
- **Robustness in footnotes.** The body states each robustness result in one sentence and
  points to the Internet Appendix, which has about twenty tables. Weighting and clustering
  are stated once in a footnote and then kept the same throughout.
- **Calibrated language.** The heterogeneity results "may alleviate (though not
  eliminate)" concerns about omitted variables. Hedges like that one show readers the
  authors know where the evidence stops.
- **Policy that follows from the finding.** The policy point concerns speed: fraud
  spreading through networks outran the program's pay-now, chase-later model. That
  conclusion depends on the spread result, so it does not read as an afterthought.

### Where the specimen is thin

A referee reading the paper with @sec-graph-exposure open would press on three points.
First, linked places can be *targeted* together, for example by social media
advertising. That is a common shock that travels along ties, and none of the tests
separates it from person-to-person transmission. Second, the network is measured in 2021,
after the program began, so the design assumes ties predate the fraud. Third, the Oster
bound depends on the assumed maximum $R^2$ (@sec-causal-oster), and the paper uses one
value. None of these sinks the paper, but a manuscript of this genre should raise each
point itself, in Section 3.5's list, before the referee does.

### Carrying the template into a marketing journal

The same skeleton fits a word-of-mouth or adoption paper using place-level outcomes and
the public county-to-county Social Connectedness Index [@bailey2018connectedness]. The
contribution paragraph should name which of four evidence types the paper supplies,
because marketing referees will rank them. A shock to the network itself, as in
@dimmock2018fraud's use of firm mergers, ranks highest. Next comes a shock to one's
contacts that does not touch oneself, as in @bailey2018housing. A fingerprint outcome
ranks third, as in @maturana2019teachers's same-lender choices among teachers. A stacked
falsification battery alone comes last. The specimen combines the third and fourth. Say
plainly which ones you have, and title the effect accordingly: "social transmission is
consistent with" is a defensible claim from a battery, "the causal peer effect is" is not.

::: {.callout-tip}
## A checklist for the observational contagion paper

1. Ask the question in the title; if a well-known paper asked it in another setting,
   echo that title.
2. State rival hypotheses before the favored one, with the prediction each makes, and
   give the rivals a real test.
3. Show the raw variation (maps, within-unit spread, time paths) before any regression.
4. Define the exposure measure as an equation, and exclude the nearest units (own county,
   own firm) so it cannot be mechanical.
5. Report magnitude in a portable unit: standardized coefficients plus incremental $R^2$.
6. Build the spine (@tbl-sw-contagion-spine): one heading per referee worry, one exhibit
   per heading.
7. Name the reflection problem explicitly, concede what cannot be ruled out, then list
   your responses.
8. Find at least one fingerprint outcome that only shared information could produce.
9. Add qualitative evidence of what was transmitted, with the raw material in an appendix.
10. State weighting, clustering and standardization once, and keep them fixed across
    tables. Standardized coefficients change with the standardization sample.
11. Rank your evidence type against shock-based designs and phrase the causal claim to
    match.
:::

## The Theory-Building Paper: Naming a Construct from Hidden Data {#sec-sw-theory-building}

Some papers earn their place by changing how a field looks at a phenomenon. They name
a construct nobody had named, show how to observe it, sort its variants, and end with
what institutions should do about it. This is the inductive theory-building paper. It
is the house genre of *Organization Science*, *Administrative Science Quarterly*, and
the *Academy of Management Journal*, and marketing journals publish it too, in consumer
culture theory and in conceptual-empirical work. It is hard to learn from the
hypothesis-testing template, because the contribution is not an estimate. It is a
concept, a classification of the concept's forms, and an argument about where a
boundary lies.

@weiss2026criminal is a clean specimen. The authors ask how entrepreneurs carry out
criminal deception, meaning the use of deceptive means to defraud audiences. They answer
from the court records of 12 Silicon Valley technology ventures whose founders were
prosecuted for securities, wire, or bank fraud between 2000 and 2023. The answer is a
new construct, *façading*. Entrepreneurs construct, perform, and protect an illusory
appearance of a high-growth venture that masks the venture's actual underperformance,
and they do it in three forms keyed to how far the venture has fallen behind what its
audiences expect. The paper closes with remedies addressed to the SEC, to investors, and
to entrepreneurship educators. (This section was written from the authors' accepted
manuscript [@weiss2026criminalpreprint]. Section and table numbers follow that version
and may differ slightly in print.)

### The spine: one construct, three sub-processes, three forms

The paper makes ten moves, and each one transfers to other topics.

| Move | Where it sits | What @weiss2026criminal do | What to copy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Name an unstudied trajectory | Introduction | Prior work treats deception as dramatized storytelling. The unstudied path is the slide from dramatization into criminal deception | Place the phenomenon on a continuum the field already accepts, and point to the segment nobody has studied |
| Anchor in public cases | Introduction | Nikola's demo truck rolled down a slope; Frank fabricated a customer dataset ten times its real size | Open with one or two named public examples before the anonymized data |
| Choose a lens that spans two literatures | Introduction; Theoretical Motivation | The discourse–organizing interface. Cultural entrepreneurship studies the stories, wrongdoing research studies causes and effects, and neither studies the organizing that makes a lie hold up | Show that each literature owns half the phenomenon. Borrow the distinction from precedent (their footnote 1) instead of coining one |
| Get past the observability barrier | Methods: Dataset | Federal court records from PACER, filtered by statute, district, venture age, and funding type | Find the archive in which the hidden behavior was forced into the open, and write the sample as a filter someone could rerun |
| Define the construct from an existing one | Introduction; Data Analysis | *Façade*, an established organizational concept, becomes *façading*, a process with three sub-processes | Start from a definition readers accept, extend it, and give the extension parts a coder can find |
| Operationalize the parts | Data Analysis, Steps 2–4 | Facets deceived (narrow: one or two; expansive: more), audience (novice or expert), protection approach | Turn every part of the definition into a coding rule |
| Explain the variation | Data Analysis, Step 5; Table 3 | The form of façading tracks the size of the expectation–reality gap, which tracks the venture's life-cycle stage | Name the one dimension that sorts the cases, and report the rival explanations checked first |
| Report findings as a grid | Findings | Three forms × three sub-processes, in the same order in every subsection | Give every cell of the typology the same internal structure |
| Draw the theory | Figure 1 | Expected and actual performance over the life cycle, with the gap shaded | Make the construct a visible quantity in one picture |
| Turn mechanism into remedy | Practical Implications | Whistleblower protection for startup employees, SEC audits of late-stage ventures, investor accountability, education | Derive each remedy from a finding, and address it to a named institution |

: The architecture of an inductive theory-building paper, read from @weiss2026criminal. {#tbl-sw-theory-spine}

### Seeing something new

The paper's new way of looking rests on three reframings, and none of them needs new
vocabulary.

1. *From discourse to the discourse–organizing interface.* Earlier work studied the
   stories entrepreneurs tell. This paper studies the organizing that lets a false story
   survive checking: the doctored invoices, forged term sheets, staged demos, and
   impersonated reference calls.
2. *From the future to the past.* The earlier literature treats deception as part of
   future-making, in the form of aspirational claims about what a venture will do. The
   prosecuted founders fabricated what the venture had already done: booked revenue,
   recurring customers, a completed audit. The authors argue that fictionalizing the past
   is the hallmark of the criminal form.
3. *From the entrepreneur to the institution.* Silicon Valley's unicorn ideal sets what
   audiences expect at each stage, so the gap founders backfill is set by the ecosystem,
   not only by their own pitches.

Each reframing is a contrast a referee can check against the literature cited, and that
is what makes it defensible. A lens the referee cannot check against prior work reads as
a label.

Positioning against the nearest neighbor takes one clause. The paper cites a 2022
working paper by Mohliver, Karp, and Zuzul titled *Dominant Deceptions*, which appears
to be an earlier version of @zuzul2026dominant. That project follows a single venture
and traces how deception spreads inside it. @weiss2026criminal describe that work as being about how deception
diffuses within ventures, and they claim a different question: how deception is carried
out, compared across ventures. Both papers build on an expectation–reality gap, and their
answers fit together. One traces the drift from "we will" to "we have" inside one firm.
The other sorts the finished schemes across firms. When a close competitor exists, name
it, say which question it answers, and claim a different one.

### Defining the construct

The definition is built in three steps. It starts from a noun the field already uses. In
the organizational definition the authors adopt, a façade is a symbolic front that
reassures stakeholders of the organization's legitimacy. The noun then becomes a
process, façading. Finally, the process is split into sub-processes a coder can find in a
document:

- *constructing* the façade, through fictionalized stories, fabricated evidence, staged
  product demos, co-opted verification, and manipulated regulatory compliance;
- *performing* it before the audiences that hold resources;
- *protecting* it from scrutiny.

A construct also needs a boundary, because a construct defined only by its center gets
stretched to fit everything (@sec-construct-vs-variable). The paper draws the line
between ordinary entrepreneurial dramatization and criminal deception. Entrepreneurs
cross it when their stories become detached from the venture's operational reality and
are propped up by organized fabrication of evidence. That boundary is what makes the
construct useful, because it tells an educator, an investor, or a juror which side of the
line a given act falls on.

The typology is cumulative. Surface façading fictionalizes stories of imminent success.
Reinforced façading adds interlocking sets of faked historical evidence and central
control of information. Deep façading adds faked product demos, co-opted due diligence,
manipulated regulatory compliance, and organized secrecy. Each form contains the acts of
the one before it (their Table 3). That makes the scheme easy to apply and hard to
dispute at the margins. The authors also report what they did not see. They call the
process discontinuous because no venture in the data moved from one form to the next,
and they say such a progression is possible but unobserved.

### Measuring it: data that make the hidden visible

Criminal deception is hidden by design, which is why earlier research theorized it mostly
through its causes and consequences. The paper's main methodological move is to find data
in which the hidden part is already documented. Court records are produced adversarially.
Prosecutors must prove each deceptive act with exhibits, and defendants contest the
evidence. The sample is defined as a filter a reader could rerun:

- federal securities-fraud charges and the related wire, bank, and conspiracy statutes;
- the Northern District of California;
- cases between 2000 and 2023;
- privately held, equity-financed, high-growth technology ventures;
- fraud within ten years of founding.

The filter excludes public companies, fraud tied to an IPO, and SEC investigations that
settled or closed without a public record. A second search then collects every further
case against the same founders.

The analysis section is unusually long, and the authors say why: inductive analysis of
court records is rare in organization science. It has five steps:

1. selecting documents (complaints, indictments, plea agreements, sentencing memoranda,
   and trial transcripts, but not procedural filings);
2. in vivo coding of the first three ventures;
3. building a codebook by moving between the data and the literature;
4. drawing a timeline for each venture, with its funding rounds overlaid;
5. comparing the twelve cases.

Two choices are worth copying. In the last step, the authors built tables to test rival
explanations before settling on the life-cycle gap. They checked whether sophistication
depended on how early the deception began, and on how long it lasted. They also
pseudonymized every venture although the records are public, because the aim is patterns
across cases, not singling out deviant individuals.

The headline numbers in the introduction can be checked against the paper's own Table 1.
Run this check on your own manuscript before you submit it.

```{r sw-facading-audit}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# The 12 ventures of Weiss & Radoynovska (2026), from their Tables 1 and 3.
# capital_musd: equity capital raised, $ million. prison_months: summed over all
# defendants (founders, co-founders, executives); 0 = civil case only; NA = pending.
cases <- data.frame(
  venture = c("Speedify", "TakeOff", "RapidLauncher",
              "QuickSnap", "ProfitDash", "Accelify", "RevenueBoost",
              "ScaleX", "Tracton", "UnicornHealth", "HyperJet", "GrowthHacker"),
  form = factor(rep(c("Surface", "Reinforced", "Deep"), c(3, 4, 5)),
                levels = c("Surface", "Reinforced", "Deep")),
  capital_musd  = c(12, 22, 1.13, 115.7, 4.5, 204.5, 7.3,
                    910.41, 17.6, 104.79, 93.77, 0.30),
  court_cases   = c(1, 1, 1, 3, 1, 1, 1, 6, 2, 3, 5, 2),   # appeals counted as cases
  prison_months = c(0, 24, 8, 18, 36, 0, 88, 135 + 155, 30, NA, 180 + 160, 36),
  pages         = c(28, 64, 53, 153, 58, 25, 94, 2702, 68, 135, 521, 121)
)

# Audit the introduction's headline totals against the table.
data.frame(
  quantity   = c("Ventures", "Court cases", "Prison sentences (years)",
                 "Equity capital raised ($ million)"),
  stated     = c(12, 27, 73, 1800),
  from_table = c(nrow(cases), sum(cases$court_cases),
                 sum(cases$prison_months, na.rm = TRUE) / 12,
                 sum(cases$capital_musd))
)

# How much of the coded evidence each form of facading rests on.
by_form <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cases, cases$form), function(d) data.frame(
  form           = as.character(d$form[1]),
  ventures       = nrow(d),
  median_capital = median(d$capital_musd),
  court_pages    = sum(d$pages),
  share_of_pages = round(sum(d$pages) / sum(cases$pages), 2)
)))
rownames(by_form) <- NULL
by_form
```

Three of the four totals reproduce: 12 ventures, 27 court cases (counting appeals as
cases), and 72.5 prison-years, which the introduction rounds to 73. The capital raised
does not. The per-venture figures sum to \$1.49 billion against \$1.8 billion in the text,
and we could not reconcile the two. The published version may have corrected one or the
other. The \$687.6 million in losses cannot be rebuilt from the table at all. Table 1 mixes
restitution, disgorgement, and forfeiture, and two co-founders owe the same \$93 million in
restitution. The rule for your own paper is that every number in the introduction should
be recomputable from a table in the paper, with the aggregation rule stated in the table
note.

The page counts carry a second lesson. Deep-façading cases supply 88% of the 4,022 coded
pages, and ScaleX, the one venture whose founder went to a jury trial, supplies 2,702
pages by itself. The most sophisticated form is therefore observed through the deepest
records, and records are deepest where a defendant fought the charges. A referee could
fairly ask whether part of what separates the forms is documentation rather than
behavior, since a guilty plea leaves a thin file. The rival explanations the authors
report concern timing and duration, not record depth. If your data source's coverage
varies with your construct, say so, and show that the construct holds among cases with
comparable records.

The gap itself can be measured with numbers, which points to a quantitative follow-up.
Where a complaint quotes a claimed figure beside the true one, their ratio measures how
far the façade had drifted from reality.

```{r sw-facading-gap}
# Claimed versus actual figures quoted from the complaints in the findings section.
gap <- data.frame(
  venture = c("QuickSnap", "Accelify", "HyperJet"),
  form    = c("Reinforced", "Reinforced", "Deep"),
  metric  = c("Revenue, Q1 2018 ($)", "Gross revenue, 2013 ($ million)",
              "Client accounts, mid-2009"),
  claimed = c(6043369, 101, 1012002),
  actual  = c(1300381, 9.5, 81618)
)
gap$inflation <- round(gap$claimed / gap$actual, 1)
gap
```

Three ventures, each measured at a different stage and on a different metric, do not
make a test. Collected across hundreds of SEC complaints, a ratio like this would let
the paper's central proposition be tested: that deception becomes more elaborate as the
gap widens.

### Findings as a grid

Each findings subsection has the same internal order:

1. an opening paragraph that places the form in the life cycle and states the size of
   the gap;
2. three parts, on constructing, performing, and protecting the façade, each headed by
   a run-in sentence that states the finding (for example, "Protecting the façade
   through passing blame");
3. a closing paragraph that restates the form in one sentence and leads into the next
   form.

Each subsection draws on three to five ventures. The evidence is block quotations from
complaints, sentencing memoranda, and plea agreements. Evidence that would only repeat
what the previous form already showed goes to an online appendix (footnotes 6 and 9 say
so), and the main text shows only what is new at each level. A reader can turn to any
cell of the three-by-three grid and find the same structure.

### Drawing the theory

The paper's Figure 1 puts the theory in one picture. The venture life cycle runs along
the horizontal axis and performance up the vertical one. A steep curve, topped with a
unicorn icon, marks the performance audiences expect. A lower curve, ending in a horse
icon, marks actual performance. The area between them is shaded and widens from left to
right, and the three forms of façading label three regions of it. Breaks in the
expectation curve encode the claim that ventures enter a form directly rather than
passing through all three. @fig-sw-facading lays out the argument the figure compresses.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-sw-facading
%%| fig-cap: "The argument of Weiss and Radoynovska (2026), drawn as a chain. Their own Figure 1 plots it as two diverging performance curves. Solid arrows are the theorized relations; dashed arrows mark where the proposed remedies intervene."
flowchart TD
    E["Institutional expectations<br/><i>unicorn ideal; burden of proof<br/>rises with life-cycle stage</i>"] --> G["Expectation–reality gap<br/><i>minor · wide · extreme</i>"]
    A["Actual venture<br/>performance"] --> G
    G --> F["Form of façading<br/><i>surface · reinforced · deep</i>"]
    F --> C["Construct<br/><i>stories → faked records →<br/>staged demos, co-opted checks</i>"]
    C --> P["Perform<br/><i>novice → expert audiences</i>"]
    P --> Pr["Protect<br/><i>blame → information control →<br/>organized secrecy</i>"]
    Pr --> D["Unmasking<br/><i>insiders, probing counterparties</i>"]
    R["Remedies<br/><i>whistleblowers, audits,<br/>due diligence, education</i>"] -.-> D
    R -.-> E
    style F fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#1a73e8
```

### Contributions: arguments first, then literatures

The discussion opens with a subsection titled "Toward a Theory of Criminal Deception".
It states four numbered arguments before it mentions any literature:

1. Façading backfills the gap between expected and actual performance.
2. The form of façading depends on the size of the gap.
3. The theory sits at the discourse–organizing interface.
4. The venture's projected appearance becomes progressively detached from its reality.

The fourth argument climbs a ladder of metaphors: a veneer laid over the real venture,
then a standalone artifact that audiences deal with instead of the venture, then a staged
parallel world like the one in *The Truman Show*. Each metaphor names a different level
of detachment, so the ladder adds content rather than decoration.

Only then come the contributions, one subsection for each of three literatures (cultural
entrepreneurship, organizational wrongdoing, and the social effects of entrepreneurship),
and each ends with a research agenda. One claim is built to be quoted and argued with:
verifiability, not authenticity, is the right guard against deception, because
authenticity judgments reward the rule-breaking and hubris that entrepreneurial culture
already prizes. A contrarian claim that can be tested is often the sentence later papers
cite.

### Proposing a solution

The practical implications say who should act and how. Lower the barriers to
whistleblowing, and extend SEC whistleblower protection to startup employees. Introduce
SEC audits of ventures late in the life cycle. Hold investors who sit on boards more
accountable, and have them check claims against several independent sources during due
diligence. Teach entrepreneurship students where permissible dramatization ends and
criminal façading begins. The remedies also enter a live debate in legal scholarship over
whether the SEC should police private markets, which gives the paper readers beyond its
own field.

The remedies persuade because they follow from the findings. @tbl-sw-remedy-mirror sets
each protection approach beside what defeated it in the cases and the remedy that would
make that outcome more likely. We compiled the middle column from the findings section;
the paper does not tabulate how each façade was unmasked.

| Form | Protection approach | How the façade was unmasked | Remedy it motivates |
|---|---|---|---|
| Surface | Passing blame | A novice investor's lawyer ran a reference check (TakeOff); an intern spotted doctored wire confirmations and a former employee blogged about it (RapidLauncher); the money ran out (Speedify) | Investor due diligence; education so that novice investors and employees recognize the pattern |
| Reinforced | Centralizing and controlling information | An employee reviewing the books found nonexistent customers (QuickSnap); a newly hired CFO quit within days and told the board (Accelify) | Board pressure to hire independent finance staff; whistleblower protection for startup employees |
| Deep | Entrenching organized secrecy | Employees went to regulators and the press (ScaleX); insurers questioned the billing (UnicornHealth); the general counsel, asking a KPMG contact about CFO candidates, learned the audit had never happened (HyperJet) | Whistleblower protection; SEC audits late in the life cycle; verification that bypasses the founder |

: Each protection approach set beside how it failed in the cases and the remedy it motivates. Forms and protection approaches follow @weiss2026criminal, Table 3. The unmasking column is our compilation from their findings section; the main text does not describe it for ProfitDash, RevenueBoost, Tracton, or GrowthHacker. {#tbl-sw-remedy-mirror}

Insiders unmasked five of the eight façades whose unmasking the findings describe: an
intern, an employee, a new CFO, employees who went to regulators and the press, and a
general counsel. That pattern is the empirical case for putting whistleblowers first,
and a reader can see it in the evidence without being told. The paper does not test any
remedy, which is acceptable in *Organization Science*, where practical implications
follow from the theory. Marketing's policy outlets set a higher bar
(@sec-policy-papers-marketing). There a remedy should be evaluated, or at least costed,
before it is recommended.

### Carrying the template into a marketing journal

Marketing has its own archives in which hidden behavior was forced into the open. FTC
complaints and consent orders, National Advertising Division decisions, state
attorney-general actions, and class-action filings all document deceptive claims with
exhibits, as these court records do. The construct travels too. One deep-façading venture
sold "AI" insights that were partly produced by paid human workers watching videos, the
pattern now called AI washing. Greenwashing, fake reviews, and vaporware announcements
(@sec-market-entry) are other cases in which a claim and the organizing behind it can
come apart. Three adjustments help a marketing version get through review.

- **Put the market stake in front.** A marketing referee will ask what the construct
  changes for buyers, competitors, or regulators, not only for theory.
- **Pair the typology with a measure that scales.** The coding rules in
  @tbl-sw-theory-spine (facets deceived, audience, protection approach) can become
  labels for a text classifier run over thousands of enforcement documents
  (@sec-text-as-data). A claimed-to-actual ratio like the one above is a continuous
  measure of the gap. The typology then becomes a hypothesis the next study can test at
  scale.
- **State the boundary as a decision rule.** The line between dramatization and
  criminal deception has a counterpart in advertising law, the line between puffery and
  a material misrepresentation. A paper that tells readers which side of it a claim falls
  on is useful to managers and regulators alike.

### A second specimen: a construct that sits between two literatures

@giuliani2026doublefailure build the same kind of paper from a different kind of hidden
data. Their question is why workers stay at a plant they know is harming them and their
families. The site is the ILVA steel plant in Taranto, Italy, which by 2013 employed
about 12,000 workers, relied on 8,000 contractors, and produced about a quarter of
Italy's steel. Each relevant literature covers half of the case (checklist item 3
below). Organizational research treats employees as *insiders* who rationalize or go
along with wrongdoing. Research on victims and environmental justice treats communities
as *victims* seeking redress from institutions. These workers are both.

The data design deals with the main threat to an interview study of a past scandal,
which is that people reinterpret it in hindsight. The authors fixed two critical
incidents. The first was the 2008 dioxin crisis, which ended with about 1,200
contaminated sheep slaughtered. The second was a 2012 court order seizing the plant's
hot furnaces. They then built a database of workers' quotations recorded at the time:
over 3,000 pages of newspapers and books and about 17 hours of television, with each
quotation coded to its incident. Only after that did they add 56 interviews conducted
between 2020 and 2025 (about 63 hours). The 232 coded quotations show how workers'
framing changed between the two incidents, not just how they remember it.

The construct is defined by what it is not, and that is the move to copy.
*Organizational resignation* means staying while condemning the firm, as a way to
survive. The authors separate it in turn from loyalty, which defends the firm; from
complicity and rationalization, which excuse the wrongdoing; from apathy, which drops
the grievance; and from the victimhood of residents, who do not work there.
*Institutional abandonment* is the belief that no outside authority will protect the
workers. It builds up through repeated encounters with courts, regulators, and
politicians that deny or delay recognition. The *double-failure trap* is the two beliefs
reinforcing each other. The authors draw its boundary by comparison with single-failure
cases, in which one arena, such as a court or a firm committed to repair, still offers a
way out. A marketing version of the question is easy to state, although the paper does
not pose it: a customer, supplier, or employee who keeps dealing with a brand they
condemn is resigned, not loyal, and a satisfaction survey that reads continued business
as approval will classify them wrongly.

::: {.callout-tip}
## A checklist for the theory-building paper

1. Place the phenomenon on a continuum the field already studies, and name the segment
   nobody has studied.
2. Open with one or two named public cases before the anonymized data.
3. Show that each relevant literature holds half of the phenomenon, and borrow the lens
   from an existing distinction.
4. Find data in which the hidden behavior is already documented, and write the sample
   as a filter someone could rerun.
5. Build the construct from a definition readers accept, split it into sub-processes a
   coder can find, and state the boundary where it stops applying.
6. Make the typology cumulative if you can, and say which transitions you did not
   observe.
7. Report the rival explanations you checked, and check whether the depth of your data
   varies with the construct.
8. Give every cell of the typology the same structure in the findings, and move
   repeated evidence to an appendix.
9. Draw the construct as a quantity in one figure.
10. State the theoretical arguments before the contributions to each literature, and
    end each contribution with a research agenda.
11. Derive each remedy from a finding, address it to a named institution, and say
    whether it was tested.
12. Make every headline number recomputable from a table in the paper.
:::

## The Measurement Paper: A New Variable from Text {#sec-sw-measurement}

A measurement paper names something that matters and that no dataset records, builds a
variable for it from a source nobody had mined for that purpose, and then spends most
of its pages showing that the variable behaves the way the thing itself should. The
contribution is the variable. The regressions are there to earn the reader's trust in
it, and none of them needs to identify a causal effect. Finance and accounting publish
this genre steadily, with text-based measures of competition, financial constraints,
corporate culture, and brand value among the well-known cases
[@li2021culture; @boustanifar2025brand], and it is the most direct route by which
unstructured data (@sec-text-as-data) becomes a top-journal paper.

@boustanifar2026intangible is a specimen worth taking apart because the method is as
simple as the genre allows. The measure is a word count. Whatever persuades the reader
therefore comes from the architecture of the paper, and that architecture can be
copied. The authors start from an accounting rule. A liability goes on the balance
sheet only if it is probable and can be reliably estimated. Anything else, such as a
pending lawsuit, a product-liability exposure, an environmental obligation, or a
false-advertising or patent-infringement claim, is disclosed in the text of the annual
report and nowhere in the numbers. They call these obligations *intangible
liabilities* (IL), count the words that signal them in every 10-K filed between fiscal
years 1996 and 2020, and show that the count predicts lawsuits, reputational damage,
valuation, stock returns, and crash risk. (This section was written from the authors'
accepted manuscript [@boustanifar2023intangiblewp], in its April 2026 revision marked
as forthcoming in *Management Science*. Table numbers and estimates follow that version
and may differ slightly in print.)

### The spine: define, build, validate, price

| Move | Where it sits | What @boustanifar2026intangible do | What to copy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Name the construct by symmetry | Title; first paragraph | Intangible assets are valuable but off the balance sheet, and a large literature measures them. Intangible liabilities are the unmeasured mirror image | Find the empty cell next to a construct the field already accepts. The reader then needs no persuading that the new one is real |
| Open with a case in which the gap is visible | Epigraphs | 3M faced earplug litigation that one bank analyst put between \$2 billion and \$185 billion, and had reserved nothing, because it judged the liability neither probable nor estimable | Show one case where the standard data say zero and everyone knows the answer is not zero |
| Explain why the source contains the construct | Section 2.2 | Disclosure is legally required, and firms tend to over-disclose, vaguely, to protect themselves from plaintiffs | Argue the data-generating process of the source before measuring anything. Who writes it, under what obligation, with what incentive to shade it? |
| Build the simplest defensible measure | Section 2.2; Appendix Table 1 | Start from the 904-word litigious list of @loughran2011liability, delete 407 words, add 72, and publish all 569 terms | Start from a published instrument, document every deletion and addition with examples, and print the whole instrument |
| Check that it sorts known groups | Section 3 | Tobacco, insurance, healthcare, and pharmaceuticals rank highest. Textiles, printing, and apparel rank lowest | Show a ranking the reader could have guessed. An unsurprising figure is the point of this step |
| Show it is not only the known groups | Sections 3–4 | Industry effects alone explain 13% of the variation. 3M sits in a low-IL industry | Report how much variance the obvious classifier leaves over. That remainder is the measure's reason to exist |
| Predict an outcome the construct should cause | Section 5 | Higher IL this year, more class actions and worse media coverage next year, including within firm | Use future outcomes from an independent source, and repeat the test with unit fixed effects |
| Show that someone pays for it | Sections 5–7 | Lower valuation ratios, higher expected returns, higher crash risk, higher cost of debt and audit fees | Tie the measure to a price or a decision, so that the construct has stakes |
| Separate it from its neighbors | Appendix | The result survives controls for two litigation-risk measures and four intangible-capital measures | Enter the closest existing measures in the same regression |
| Open the box | Sections 8 and 10 | Risk-factor text and the rest of the filing both carry signal. A LASSO names the most predictive terms | Show where in the source the signal lives and which components drive it |

: The architecture of a text-based measurement paper, read from @boustanifar2026intangible. {#tbl-sw-measurement-spine}

The abstract follows the same order at one sentence per step: the accounting rule,
examples, the name, the measure, its correlates, what it predicts, how it is priced,
and the implication. A reader who stops after the abstract already knows what the
construct is and why it has stakes. That matters more in this genre than in most,
because there is no clever identification strategy to carry the reader's interest.

### Defining the construct before measuring it

The definition is borrowed from a rule, which makes the boundary of the construct
checkable. An intangible liability is an economically significant obligation that fails
the recognition test (probable and estimable) and so appears only in text. A footnote
then separates it from the neighboring accounting category. Disclosed contingent
liabilities are a subset, because a firm can be exposed to a kind of harm, such as
personal injury from its products, before any claim exists, and that exposure is
written up under risk factors. The footnote is also the argument for measuring over the
whole filing. A measure built only on the legal-proceedings section would capture the
subset and miss the construct.

A second footnote settles what "intangible" means. It is not "cannot be touched." It is
"cannot be appraised at an actual or approximate value." Human capital can be touched
and is off the balance sheet. A firm's cryptocurrency cannot be touched and is on it.
Two sentences of this kind close off the most likely misreading of a new label, and a
new construct should always get them (@sec-construct-vs-variable).

The positioning against prior work is equally short. Accounting research already
measures *litigation risk*, the probability of being sued [@kim2012litigation]. The
authors grant that it is one source of intangible liabilities and list others that it
leaves out: pending suits, recalls, guarantees, environmental obligations, and pending
legislation. They later add litigation-risk measures as controls. The claim is that the
new construct is broader than its nearest neighbor, and the paper supports the claim
with a definition in the front and a regression in the back.

### Building the measure, and the three decisions inside a word count

A dictionary measure looks like it involves no decisions. This one involves three, and
the paper defends each.

*Which words.* The starting list was built to measure tone, so many of its entries are
legalistic words with no bearing on obligations (*hereby*, *shall*, *aforementioned*).
The authors read how each word is used in filings before deciding. *Interrogate*
appears in biotech filings about interrogating cells. *Designator* is an airline code.
*Extracorporeal* is a medical procedure. All three go. The parent list is also
unigram-only and correctly omits *liability*, which is neutral in a financial
statement. The new list adds bigrams such as *product liability*, *environmental
liability*, *false advertising*, and *filed suit*, which carry the meaning that the
single word does not. For a marketing reader, the dictionary is in part a list of
marketing-made obligations: *false advertising*, *deceptive*, *product liability*,
*recall*, *warranty defect*, *counterfeit*, *unfair competition*.

*How to weight.* Every term counts equally. The cited justification is a comparison of
methods in the disclosure literature, which finds equal-weighted, domain-specific word
counts about as powerful as more elaborate schemes, provided the list excludes words
that also appear in other contexts [@henry2016tone]. That is why so much of the effort
goes into pruning.

*How to scale.* The main measure is the log of the raw count, with the log of filing
length entered as a control. The authors argue against the usual share-of-words
scaling. In sentiment work every word is positive, negative, or neutral, so a share is
natural. Here the researcher is looking for one kind of content inside a document that
is mostly about other things, and dividing by length lets differences in length drive
the variation. Where a control is impossible, as in portfolio sorts, they fall back on
the share.

The scaling decision has consequences that a short simulation makes visible. In their
Table 3 the coefficient of the log count on log filing length is about 1.2, so
dictionary hits grow faster than the filing does. The simulation below builds that in.
It is our illustration and uses no data from the paper. Each filing has a latent
exposure that the researcher never sees, a length, and a count of dictionary hits that
depends on both. The outcome depends on exposure and, separately and negatively, on
length.

```{r sw-measurement-scaling}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# A stylized illustration written for this section; none of it is the paper's data.
set.seed(41)
n      <- 20000
theta  <- rnorm(n)                         # latent exposure, never observed
len    <- 10 + 0.74 * rnorm(n)             # log words in the filing
count  <- rpois(n, exp(4.3 + 0.5 * theta + 1.2 * (len - 10)))   # dictionary hits
y      <- 1.0 * theta - 0.5 * (len - 10) + rnorm(n, sd = 3)     # long filings do worse

z <- function(x) as.numeric(scale(x))
log_count <- log(1 + count)
share     <- count / exp(len)
resid_ct  <- resid(lm(log_count ~ len))    # log count net of filing length

slope <- function(f) unname(coef(lm(f))[2])
scaling <- data.frame(
  measure = c("Log count, no length control", "Share of total words",
              "Log count, length controlled", "Latent exposure (infeasible)"),
  cor_with_exposure = c(cor(log_count, theta), cor(share, theta),
                        cor(resid_ct, theta), 1),
  cor_with_length   = c(cor(log_count, len), cor(share, len),
                        cor(resid_ct, len), cor(theta, len)),
  slope_per_sd      = c(slope(y ~ z(log_count)), slope(y ~ z(share)),
                        slope(y ~ z(resid_ct) + len), slope(y ~ z(theta) + len))
)
scaling[-1] <- round(scaling[-1], 2)
print(scaling, row.names = FALSE)
```

The raw log count is mostly a measure of how long the filing is, and its slope on the
outcome is close to zero because the length effect cancels the exposure effect. The
share does much better, but it still loads on length, because hits grow faster than
words, and it recovers only about three-quarters of the true slope. The log count with
length controlled comes close to the infeasible benchmark. Two things follow for anyone
building a count-based measure. Estimate the elasticity of the count to document length
before choosing a scaling, since a share is right only when that elasticity is one. And
when two versions of the measure appear in one paper, say which result rests on which.

### The validation ladder

The paper never claims that its dictionary is accurate. It shows, one test at a time,
that the measure sits where the construct should sit among other variables. That is a
nomological argument (@sec-reliability-validity), and laid out as a ladder it reads as
follows.

| Rung | The question a referee asks | Evidence | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| Face validity | Does it rank groups the way I would? | Mean IL across the 49 Fama–French industries | Tobacco, insurance, healthcare, and pharmaceuticals on top. Utilities sixth, traced by hand to cases such as PG&E's wildfire liabilities |
| Case validity | Does it find the firms I know about? | Top firms inside low-IL industries | 3M in business supplies, Corteva in agriculture. HP scores high and IBM low |
| Incremental variance | Is it just industry and size? | Regressions of IL on firm characteristics | Industry alone explains 13%. Industry, year, and size explain about half |
| Convergent correlates | Does it move with the known proxies? | Same regressions | Higher volatility and turnover, lower ROA, abnormal returns, and Tobin's $q$, matching the inputs to existing litigation-risk models |
| Prediction, legal | Does it forecast the event? | Securities class actions filed in the next year | 0.32% of bottom-quintile firm-years and 5.66% of top-quintile ones. One SD of IL adds 1.64 points to a 2.2% base rate, and the result holds within firm |
| Prediction, reputational | Does a different source agree? | RepRisk index of negative media coverage in the next year | One SD of IL adds 2.2 points to a mean of 10.4 |
| Valuation | Do investors see it? | Log P/E and log market-to-book | One SD of IL goes with ratios 4–5% lower |
| Pricing | Do investors demand payment for it? | Quintile portfolios and Fama–MacBeth regressions | High minus low earns 4.35% a year. Alphas run from 2.91% ($q^5$) to 6.02%. One SD of IL goes with 0.16% a month, with 19 other predictors controlled |
| Mechanism | Why would it be priced? | Firm-specific crash risk in the next year | One SD of IL raises negative skewness by 14% of its mean. Earnings surprises show no sign of mispricing |
| Discriminant | Is it an old measure renamed? | Litigation-risk and intangible-capital controls | The IL coefficient is stable. In the return regressions the litigation-risk measures do not survive the full controls |

: The validation ladder in @boustanifar2026intangible, with estimates from the accepted manuscript. {#tbl-sw-measurement-ladder}

Four features of the ladder are worth copying beyond the list itself.

1. *The outcomes come from somewhere else.* Lawsuits come from a law-school
   clearinghouse, reputation from a commercial media-screening vendor, and returns from
   the exchange. None of them is built from 10-K text, so the measure cannot predict
   them by construction.
2. *Every test is run twice, across firms and within firm.* The within-firm version
   says that when a firm's own filings add liability language, lawsuits and bad press
   follow. That answers the objection that the measure only identifies a type of firm.
3. *The descriptive tables are allowed to disagree with the thesis.* In the raw
   quintile means, valuation ratios rise with IL. The negative relation appears only
   once size, profitability, and industry are held fixed. The authors print the raw
   table, say that it shows a positive association, and then show the regression. A
   referee who finds that reversal unaided will distrust the paper. A referee who is
   told about it will not.
4. *The pricing result is given a reason.* A return premium invites the charge of data
   mining (@sec-mf-anomaly-baserate). The paper answers with a risk story, that these
   liabilities can crystallize suddenly, and tests an implication of the story on a
   different outcome, crash risk. It then tests the rival story, mispricing, on
   earnings announcements, and concedes that the two cannot be fully separated.

### Opening the authors' data: what the term counts show {#sec-sw-measurement-package}

The paper's replication package, available from the journal's supplemental-material
page, includes the count of every dictionary term in every filing, together with the
Stata logs behind each table. The return, accounting, and reputation data are licensed
and not included, so the regressions cannot be rerun from the package alone. Two checks
