are still possible. The first is against the logs. They reproduce the means and standard deviations in the manuscript's descriptive
table, and the twelve portfolio alphas to within 0.03 percentage points, so the estimates quoted in this section match the authors' final
runs. The second is on the measure itself. The script
`replication/intangible-liabilities/il_measure_checks.R` in this book's repository
computes the statistics below from the term counts, over all 232,874 filings from
32,604 filers with fiscal years 1996 to 2020. That is the full set of filings scored,
about twice the 112,457 firm-years that survive the match to stock and accounting data,
so the figures describe the measure before any sample selection. They are our
calculations and appear nowhere in the paper.

| Question | Result in the term counts |
|---|---|
| How fast does the count grow with filing length? | Elasticity of 1.16, and 1.11 with year and two-digit industry effects. Length alone explains 66% of the variance of the log count |
| How much is industry? | Two-digit industry effects alone explain 12%, close to the paper's 13% |
| How concentrated is the count? | Ten terms supply 43% of all hits: *claims*, *legal*, *court*, *settlement*, *litigation*, *contingent*, *judgment*, *claim*, *penalties*, *damages*. Fourteen terms supply half, and 51 of the 569 supply 80% |
| Does the measure depend on those ten? | Net of length and year, the measure without the top ten terms correlates 0.94 with the full measure |
| How much comes from marketing-origin terms? | *False advertising*, *deceptive*, *product liability*, *recall*, *warranty*, *counterfeit*, *unfair competition*, and *misrepresentation* supply 1.4% of hits. An index built from them alone correlates 0.28 with the full measure |
| Is it a firm trait or a yearly signal? | Net of length, year, and industry, 63% of the variance is between firms. Net of length and year, the year-to-year correlation within a firm is 0.86 |

: Properties of the intangible-liabilities count, computed from the filing-level term counts in the authors' replication package. {#tbl-sw-measurement-package}

Three lessons follow, and each one is a check any dictionary paper can run on itself.

*A dictionary of 569 terms is, in use, a dictionary of about 50.* Zipf's law guarantees
that a few frequent terms dominate any count. The ten that dominate here are the most
generic words on the list, and *legal* appears in nearly every filing. The measure survives
their removal almost unchanged, which is reassuring, and it is the kind of evidence a
reader wants in the paper: a table of the top terms with their share of hits, and the
measure recomputed without them.

*A sub-construct can be nearly invisible inside the total.* The marketing-made
obligations are in the dictionary, but they carry 1.4% of the count and move largely
independently of it. A researcher who wants product-harm or false-advertising exposure
should build that index separately and validate it separately. The full measure is
mostly a litigation-and-contingency measure.

*Check the named cases under both scalings.* The paper contrasts IBM, with very low
intangible liabilities, and HP, with very high ones. In the fiscal-2020 counts HP has
767 hits in a filing of about 52,800 words and IBM has 77 in a filing of about 10,300
words. On the raw log count IBM sits at the 15th percentile of that year's filings and
HP at the 96th. Net of length, year, and industry, IBM rises to the 79th percentile and
HP stays at the 95th. IBM's 10-K is short, which is what one would see if much of its
annual report were incorporated by reference in exhibits that the text processing
drops, though the package cannot confirm the reason. The other named cases hold either
way: 3M, PG&E, and Corteva are above the 90th percentile on both versions, and Boston
Beer is below the 15th on both. An illustrative contrast should be chosen after
checking that it does not depend on the scaling.

### Where the specimen is thin

A template is more useful with its weak points marked, and several of them are places
where a marketing referee would press harder than a finance referee did.

- *No human has checked the measure against text.* There is no hand-coded sample of
  filings, no precision for individual terms, and no test of whether a high score means
  much liability or much boilerplate. The generic words that dominate the count
  (@tbl-sw-measurement-package) appear in filings with nothing at stake. The validation
  is entirely by association with outcomes. A
  marketing journal would normally ask for agreement with human judgment as well
  (@sec-classification-validity).
- *The simplest rival is beaten off the page.* A footnote reports that the parent
  dictionary shows no robust relation to future lawsuits, reputation, or returns. This
  is the comparison that justifies all the pruning, and it is described as unreported.
  It should be a table (@sec-sw-design-science makes the same point about method
  papers).
- *The legal outcome is narrower than the construct.* The lawsuits are securities
  class actions, which shareholders bring. The construct's own examples are product,
  environmental, and intellectual-property claims. The two are related, since a product
  disaster often triggers a shareholder suit, but the validation outcome is not the
  obligation the paper defines.
- *Filing length does a lot of work.* Adding length and three accounting ratios lifts
  the explained variance of IL from 0.51 to 0.75. In the return regressions, length
  carries a coefficient of $-0.17$ beside IL's $+0.16$. The finding is therefore about
  liability language relative to the length of the filing, and long filings alone
  predict lower returns. The simulation above shows why this must be stated plainly,
  and the IBM case shows it in the data.
- *The headline number is one of several.* The abstract's 3% matches the
  industry-adjusted figures (a 3.02% return spread and a 2.99% six-factor alpha). The
  same table gives 2.11%, significant only at the 10%
  level, under the industry-adjusted $q^5$ model and 6.02% under a mispricing-factor
  model. Announcement returns for high-IL firms are significantly negative in the two
  specifications without industry effects and insignificant with them.
- *The predictive words are hard to read.* The LASSO's 149 selected terms include
  *infringement*, *product liability*, and *fraud*, and also *majeure*, *bailiff*, and
  *attornment*. The text describes a pre-2015 training sample and a post-2015 test
  sample but reports no out-of-sample fit. The authors do warn that a zero coefficient
  does not make a word uninformative.
- *Some counts do not reconcile in the manuscript.* The text gives 112,716 firm-years
  and the descriptive table 112,457. The package's construction log settles it in favor
  of the table: 114,276 filings match the stock and accounting data, and 1,819 without
  a count are dropped. The reputation sample is 11,329 in the text and 11,256 or 12,598
  in the regressions. The final typeset version may resolve these. The lesson from @sec-sw-theory-building applies here too: every sample size in the
  prose should be recomputable from a table.

None of this undoes the contribution. It marks what a successor paper can add, and the
authors' own conclusion lists two of the items: more sources (earnings calls, social
media, press coverage) and better language models.

### Carrying the template into a marketing journal

Marketing is full of constructs that firms describe in words and no database records.
A firm's exposure to a product-harm crisis, its dependence on a few customers or one
retailer, its reliance on a celebrity or founder, its privacy and data-breach exposure,
and the gap between its sustainability claims and its operations are all discussed in
filings, earnings calls, complaints, and reviews, and none has a standard variable.
One of the authors had already applied the recipe on the asset side, with a brand
measure built from the frequency of the word *brand* in filings
[@boustanifar2025brand] (@sec-branding). Seen together, the two papers are one research
program: pick an off-balance-sheet quantity, find the text in which firms must discuss
it, count, validate, and price.

Four adjustments help a marketing version.

- **Validate against people as well as outcomes.** Have trained coders rate a few
  hundred documents on the construct, report agreement among them, and report how the
  measure tracks their ratings. Predictive tests show that a measure is useful.
  Agreement with human judgment shows that it measures what its name says
  (@sec-reliability-validity).
- **Tabulate the horse race.** Put the parent dictionary, a share-scaled version, an
  embedding-expanded dictionary (@sec-tad-culture-dictionary), and an LLM coder
  (@sec-llm-extraction) in one table with the same outcomes. If the simple count wins or
  ties, transparency is the argument for it. If it loses, the paper has a better measure.
- **Choose outcomes a marketing reader prices.** Recalls, regulatory actions,
  complaint volume, brand-tracking scores, customer churn, and retailer delistings can
  play the role that class actions and RepRisk play here. Stock returns remain
  available for a strategy audience (@sec-marketing-finance).
- **Decide what the last third of the paper is.** A finance paper ends with pricing. A
  marketing paper can end with a decision instead: which firms should change
  disclosure, product design, or claims, and what it is worth to them. If the measured
  facts raise a question that reduced-form evidence cannot settle, a small model is the
  other way to finish (@sec-sw-measure-model).

::: {.callout-tip}
## A checklist for the measurement paper

1. Name the construct by its relation to one the field already measures, and define it
   with a rule that says what is in and what is out.
2. Open with a named case in which the standard data record nothing and the stakes are
   plainly large.
3. Explain who produces the source text, under what obligation, and with what incentive
   to distort it.
4. Start from a published instrument. Document deletions and additions with examples,
   and print the full instrument in an appendix.
5. Estimate how the raw count scales with document length before choosing between a
   share and a controlled count, and say which results use which.
6. Show that the measure sorts known groups and finds known cases, then report how much
   variance those groups leave unexplained.
7. Predict future outcomes drawn from independent sources, across units and within
   unit.
8. Tie the measure to a price or a decision.
9. Put the nearest existing measures, and the parent instrument, in the same table.
   Report the top terms' share of the count and the measure recomputed without them.
10. Validate against human coding as well as against outcomes.
11. Show where in the source the signal sits and which terms carry it, with
    out-of-sample fit.
12. Print the raw descriptive pattern even when it runs against the conditional one,
    and make every sample size recomputable.
:::

## The Front End {#sec-sw-front-end}

The front end—title, abstract, and introduction—is the part of the paper most
people read and the only part most people read. It carries the entire promise–
payoff loop of @fig-sw-paper-flow in compressed form, and a reviewer's
accept-lean or reject-lean is often set before the methods section begins. The
front end deserves a disproportionate share of writing effort precisely because it
does a disproportionate share of the persuasive work.

### The title

A title's job is to name the contribution in eight to fifteen words such that the
right reader stops scrolling. It should contain the paper's key constructs (the
terms a searcher would type) and, where possible, signal the relationship the paper
establishes rather than merely the topic it addresses. "Brand Prominence and
Status Signaling" names a topic; "Signaling Status with Luxury Goods: The Role of
Brand Prominence" names a relationship and a mechanism. Question titles and
two-part titles (a hook before the colon, the substance after) are common in JCR
and JM and rarer in *Marketing Science*, reflecting the venues' different house
voices—a difference worth matching to the target journal.

### The abstract

The abstract is the most-read and least-revised 250 words in science, and the
imbalance is a mistake. It must be **self-contained**: a reader who sees only the
abstract should be able to state the paper's objective, method, principal finding,
and implication. The canonical structure mirrors @eq-sw-chain in miniature—one or
two sentences each for the problem, the approach, the result (with direction and,
where it fits, magnitude), and the "so what". Two failure modes dominate. The
**descriptive abstract** announces what the paper does ("we examine the effect of
X on Y") without ever stating what it *found*, leaving the reader no wiser; the
**overloaded abstract** crams in every robustness check and moderator, drowning the
headline. The fix for both is the same: lead with the finding.

### The introduction as a funnel

The introduction is where most rejections are decided, and it has a near-mechanical
structure: a **funnel** from the broad problem to the specific contribution. A
robust template runs problem $\rightarrow$ tension or puzzle $\rightarrow$ gap
$\rightarrow$ "in this paper we" $\rightarrow$ approach $\rightarrow$ findings
$\rightarrow$ contributions $\rightarrow$ roadmap. @fig-sw-funnel renders it.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-sw-funnel
%%| fig-cap: "The introduction funnel. Each band narrows from the world's problem to this paper's specific increment to knowledge. The 'in this paper, we...' sentence is the pivot from motivation to contribution and should appear by the end of the second page."
flowchart TD
    P["The broad problem<br/><i>why anyone should care</i>"] --> T["The tension / puzzle<br/><i>what doesn't fit</i>"]
    T --> G["The gap<br/><i>what prior work left open</i>"]
    G --> Q["<b>In this paper, we…</b><br/><i>the pivot to contribution</i>"]
    Q --> A2["Approach<br/><i>data and method, one paragraph</i>"]
    A2 --> F["Findings<br/><i>headline results, with direction</i>"]
    F --> C2["Contributions<br/><i>ΔK, stated as claims</i>"]
    C2 --> R2["Roadmap<br/><i>optional, brief</i>"]
    style Q fill:#fce8e6,stroke:#d93025
    style C2 fill:#e6f4ea,stroke:#188038
```

Two discipline points govern the funnel. First, the pivot sentence—"In this paper,
we..."—should arrive early, by the end of the second page; an introduction that is
still motivating the problem on page four has lost the reviewer. Second, the
contributions should be stated as *claims the reader will be able to accept*, not
as activities the authors performed. "We contribute by examining the role of
arousal" is an activity; "We show that empathetic responses raise gratitude even
before a service failure is resolved, which the prior literature's
resolution-centric models cannot accommodate" is a claim and an explicit
$\Delta\mathcal{K}$.

### Positioning against the literature

The literature review is not a homage to everyone who has touched the topic; it is
the construction of $\mathcal{K}_{\text{before}}$, the precise baseline against
which the contribution is measured. Its house failure mode is the **annotated
bibliography**—a serial list of "Author (year) found X; Author (year) found Y"—which
demonstrates reading but not synthesis and leaves the reviewer to infer the gap.
The remedy is to organize the review around *tensions and open questions* rather
than around papers, so that the gap emerges as the natural next move in a
conversation the reader can now follow. The house style guide's instruction to
**weave, not list** citations is exactly this principle applied at the sentence
level: each citation should earn its place by advancing the argument, and the
strongest evidence per point should crowd out the duplicative.

## Writing for the Top-4 {#sec-sw-top4}

### What rises to a top journal

The top-4 differ from solid field journals less in the correctness of the work they
publish than in the size and generality of the increment $\Delta\mathcal{K}$. The
bar that rises is **importance**: a top-4 paper must change how a non-trivial
slice of the field thinks, not merely add a brick to a narrow wall. Editors and
reviewers operationalize this in recurring questions—Would I assign this in a
doctoral seminar? Does it change what I would tell a manager? Does it open new
research, or close a question others were pursuing? A paper can be flawless and
still be rejected for answering a question too few people were asking.

The venues also have distinguishable identities, and matching the paper to the
venue is part of the craft. *Marketing Science* and JMR lean toward
methodological rigor and formal models—a structural estimator or an analytical
game-theoretic result is at home there. JCR prizes psychological process and
theory, typically established across multiple experiments that triangulate a
mechanism. JM spans substantive and managerial questions with an explicit demand
for managerial relevance. The same finding, dressed for the wrong venue, draws
reviewers who want what the paper was never built to deliver.

### Genres of contribution: many roads to the top-4

The importance bar is not cleared in a single way. Marketing is methodologically
plural, and a top journal publishes several distinct *genres* of research, each with
its own logic of contribution and its own standard of proof. Naming the genre—to
oneself first, then to the reader—matters as much as naming the paper type earlier in
this chapter, because a reviewer recruited for one genre will judge by its rules. A
working map of the traditions a marketing scholar will meet:

- **Experimental and consumer-behavior** work identifies a psychological *mechanism*
  by controlled manipulation, usually triangulated across several studies that close
  off rival accounts one at a time. The contribution is a process: not merely that $X$
  moves $Y$ but *why*.
- **Analytical / game-theoretic** work builds a deliberately stylized model and
  extracts a non-obvious, general implication from its equilibrium—why a firm might
  rationally do the counterintuitive thing. The currency is generality, not data.
- **Empirical / structural** work estimates the primitives of behavior—preferences,
  costs—under an explicit identification argument so it can run *counterfactuals* the
  raw data never ran (@sec-sm-discrete-choice). The contribution is policy-relevant
  quantities and the "what if" they license.
- **Descriptive** work documents robust, previously unseen *patterns* in novel—often
  large-scale—data, and makes *no* causal claim. The contribution is the fact itself.
- **Prescriptive / optimization** work formulates a decision problem and solves it with
  a guarantee or a demonstrably better method (@sec-sm-socpd). The contribution is a
  solvable formulation and its performance.
- **Strategy and marketing-management** work links a marketing action to firm outcomes
  and firm value with an explicit demand for managerial relevance (the JM register
  above).

These are axes, not bins: a single paper is often empirical *and* descriptive, or
analytical *and* prescriptive, and the strongest work borrows across them. But the
reader must be told which claim bears the weight, because the standard of proof differs
by genre—an identification argument is decisive for a structural paper and beside the
point for an analytical one.

The genre students most often underrate is the **descriptive**, and it repays a closer
look because its revival is one of the field's live developments. For two decades the
credibility revolution (@sec-credibility) so prized causal identification that pure
description read as second class—a table on the way to a regression. That has reversed,
for a concrete reason: platform, transaction, and sensor data now expose patterns no
prior dataset could show, and a pattern no one had seen is a genuine increment to
$\mathcal{K}$ even with no causal arrow attached. The descriptive paper still clears the
top-4 bar, but on *different* terms. It does not owe internal validity for an effect it
never claims; it owes (i) genuinely novel data, (ii) patterns robust to how the data are
sliced, (iii) a *surprise*—a fact that overturns or sharpens a belief the field held—and
(iv) scrupulous candor about what is described versus explained. Overclaiming causation
is the descriptive paper's characteristic failure; under-selling importance ("we merely
describe") is its mirror-image one.

@chen2026counterfeits is a clean specimen. From millions of cross-border orders the
authors document a *U-shaped* relationship between income and counterfeit
consumption—both low- and high-income consumers buy more fakes than the middle, with the
tails differing in composition—advancing no instrument and estimating no treatment
effect. Its title announces "A Descriptive Analysis," and its contribution is precisely
the documented gradient, which complicates the tidy poseur account of counterfeit demand
(@sec-branding). That the top journals now run short-format *Frontiers* articles for
exactly this kind of high-value description—@kaiser2026chatgpt's map of a nascent LLM
sales channel is a companion case—is institutional evidence that the genre has a settled
place. The craft lesson mirrors the framing discipline of @sec-sw-contribution: know your
genre, promise the kind of contribution it actually makes, and defend it on its own terms
rather than borrowing the rhetoric of a genre you did not practice.

@chang2026plantimagery is a second specimen, and a useful complement because it ran
as a full article without the *Frontiers* label, and because almost every
design choice in it is visible from its front matter. The question is small and
concrete: do online home listings with more pictures of plants sell for more? From
40,294 sold properties and their 569,773 listing photos on a major U.S. real-estate
platform, labelled for plant content by a multimodal language model, the authors
document that listings with more plant imagery transact at higher prices, sell
faster, and attract more online engagement, after accounting for an extensive set of
property, neighborhood, listing, and market factors. Six choices are worth copying.

1. **The title names the genre, and the claim never borrows a causal verb.** The
   one-sentence summary on the journal record says plant imagery is "associated
   with" higher valuations. A reader is told what kind of evidence to expect before
   reading a single table, which pre-empts the "where is the instrument?" review.
2. **Theory motivates the look without being put on trial.** Phytophilia, the idea
   that people are innately drawn to plant life, explains why anyone should expect a
   pattern. The paper does not claim to test it, and does not need to.
3. **A practitioner survey supplies the surprise.** The authors survey real-estate
   agents and report that awareness of plants as a staging tool, and the priority
   agents give it, are low. That converts a correlation into a fact worth knowing:
   the pattern is valuable precisely because the people who could act on it do not
   act on it. It is the descriptive paper's version of the "open question" of
   @sec-sw-open-question.
4. **Several outcomes, one direction.** Price, time on market, and online engagement
   are three outcomes with different confounds. A pattern that runs the same way in
   all three is harder to explain away than a pattern in one, and triangulation of
   this kind does part of the work that a mechanism test does in a causal paper.
5. **The conditioning set is the robustness argument.** The obvious rival account
   is that greenery proxies for bigger lots, richer neighborhoods, better
   photographers, and more effort by the seller. A descriptive paper cannot rule
   that account out with exogenous variation, so it narrows it with controls for
   property, neighborhood, listing, and market factors, and states that what
   survives is an association.
6. **Measurement is the method.** A general-purpose vision-language model makes a
   narrow visual construct codable at a scale no research assistant could match
   (@sec-image-processing). The paper's reference list (manual image-annotation
   software, CLIP, Faster R-CNN, VGG, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-5) points to a pipeline
   built with manual annotation and several competing models. Its validation is
   where a reader should look first, because a generated label is the one input a
   descriptive design cannot afford to get wrong.

The paper also cites @dekadt2025gooddescription, whose standard is a useful
checklist for anyone writing in this genre: a good descriptive question uncovers a
fact in need of explanation, builds theory, or helps evaluate theory, and a good
descriptive analysis is clear, comparable, and complete. Filled in for this paper,
the contribution sentence of @sec-sw-contribution reads: *we establish that listing
photos with more plants are associated with higher prices, faster sales, and more
engagement among U.S. homes, a pattern prior work could not document because coding
plants in half a million photos was too costly, and one practitioners do not act on.*

### Robustness as rhetoric

At the top-4, a single clean result rarely suffices; the paper must anticipate and
preempt the reviewer's alternative explanations. This is why top-4 empirical papers
carry batteries of robustness checks, alternative specifications, and—in
experimental work—multiple studies whose designs rule out competing accounts one
by one. The logic is the broken-arrow logic of @eq-sw-chain: every alternative
explanation is a way the arrow $D \Rightarrow R$ might fail, and each robustness
check is a patch that keeps the arrow intact. The writing task is to present this
defensive machinery without burying the headline—typically by stating the main
result cleanly, then organizing the defenses as a navigable sequence of named
threats and the evidence that disarms each.

> The reviewer is not your enemy; the reviewer is the proxy for every skeptical
> reader your paper will ever have. Every alternative explanation a reviewer
> raises is one a future reader would have raised silently and then disbelieved
> you. Writing the rebuttal into the paper *before* submission is simply doing the
> reviewer's job for them, and it is the single highest-return revision activity.

### The review process and the response

Top-4 papers are essentially never accepted on first submission; the modal good
outcome is a *revise and resubmit* (R&R), and the revision is where many papers are
won or lost. The response to reviewers is itself a document with its own craft. Its
governing principle is that the author's job is to make the editor's
accept-decision *easy to defend*: every reviewer comment receives a numbered,
verbatim restatement followed by a specific response and a pointer to the exact
change in the manuscript. Disagreement is permitted but must be argued with
evidence, courteously, and sparingly—an author who fights every point signals
defensiveness, while an author who concedes everything signals that the original
work was unconsidered. The art is to distinguish comments that improve the paper
(adopt them) from comments that reflect a misunderstanding (clarify the text so the
next reader does not misunderstand either) from the rare comment that is simply
wrong (rebut it with evidence and grace).

## Clarity and Revision {#sec-sw-clarity}

### Clarity as a property of the reader, not the writer

Clarity is not an ornament; it is the probability that a reader recovers the
intended meaning on the first pass. Writing that the author finds clear because the
author already knows the answer is a category error—the test of clarity is whether
a reader *who does not yet know the conclusion* can follow the argument. A few
sentence-level disciplines do most of the work, and they are mechanical enough to
apply as a checklist. Prefer the active voice and a concrete agent ("we estimate",
"the model predicts") over agentless passives that hide who did what. Put the
subject and verb early and close together so the reader is not made to hold an open
clause across half a line. Use one term for one concept—do not alternate "effect",
"impact", and "influence" for the same quantity, because the reader will hunt for a
distinction that is not there. Expand every acronym on first use and define every
construct before deploying it, a discipline the house style enforces throughout.

### Measuring readability

Readability can be measured, and while no formula substitutes for judgment, the
indices make a useful diagnostic. The **Gunning fog index** estimates the years of
formal education a reader needs to understand a passage on first reading
[@gunning1952technique]. Let a passage contain $W$ words, $S$ sentences, and $C$
"complex" words (three or more syllables, excluding common suffix inflections).
The index is

$$
\text{Fog} \;=\; 0.4\left(\frac{W}{S} \;+\; 100\,\frac{C}{W}\right),
$$ {#eq-sw-fog}

a weighted sum of average sentence length and the percentage of complex words.
The two terms encode the two main sources of difficulty—long sentences and
unfamiliar words—and the constant scales the result to a U.S. grade level, so a fog
score of 12 corresponds roughly to the reading level of a high-school senior.
Academic prose runs higher, but a methods section with a fog score in the high
teens is usually not "rigorous"; it is merely overlong in the sentence and
overloaded in the noun phrase. Textual-complexity measures of exactly this family
are now standard tools in the marketing and finance literatures for analyzing
corporate disclosures and other documents at scale [@loughran2020; @loughran2020a],
which is a useful reminder that the readability of *your* prose is itself a
measurable, and therefore improvable, quantity.

The estimator in @eq-sw-fog is a heuristic, not a model, and its assumptions are
worth stating because they tell you when it misleads. It assumes that syllable
count proxies word difficulty (false for short technical jargon like "prior" or
"yield", which are hard despite being monosyllabic) and that sentence length
proxies syntactic load (false for a long but perfectly parallel list). It is best
read as a *smoke detector*: a high score reliably indicates a problem somewhere,
but a low score does not certify clarity. The following chunk implements it and a
companion length diagnostic so the measure is reproducible rather than mystical;
@fig-sw-fog shows the score falling as the same sentence is progressively tightened.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sw-fog
#| fig-cap: "Gunning fog scores for three versions of the same sentence—a bloated original, a moderate edit, and a lean rewrite—showing how shortening sentences and replacing complex words lowers the estimated reading grade. The dashed line marks a fog score of 12 (high-school senior)."
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
set.seed(41)

# A deliberately rough syllable counter: count vowel groups per word.
# Heuristic, not linguistic ground truth -- adequate for a relative diagnostic.
count_syllables <- function(word) {
  word <- tolower(gsub("[^a-z]", "", word))
  if (nchar(word) == 0) return(0L)
  groups <- gregexpr("[aeiouy]+", word)[[1]]
  n <- if (groups[1] == -1L) 1L else length(groups)
  if (grepl("e$", word) && n > 1L) n <- n - 1L   # silent terminal 'e'
  max(n, 1L)
}

gunning_fog <- function(text) {
  sentences <- unlist(strsplit(text, "(?<=[.!?])\\s+", perl = TRUE))
  sentences <- sentences[nzchar(trimws(sentences))]
  words <- unlist(strsplit(text, "\\s+"))
  words <- words[nzchar(words)]
  W <- length(words); S <- max(length(sentences), 1L)
  syl <- vapply(words, count_syllables, integer(1))
  C <- sum(syl >= 3L)                              # "complex" words
  0.4 * (W / S + 100 * C / W)
}

versions <- c(
  bloated  = paste("The utilization of an excessively elaborate and",
                   "circumlocutory prose style, characterized by the",
                   "accumulation of subordinate clauses, demonstrably",
                   "attenuates comprehensibility for the readership."),
  moderate = paste("Using an elaborate, indirect prose style with many",
                   "subordinate clauses reduces how well readers understand",
                   "the argument."),
  lean     = "Dense prose is hard to read."
)

fog <- vapply(versions, gunning_fog, numeric(1))
print(round(fog, 1))

barplot(fog, col = "grey80", border = NA, ylab = "Gunning fog (grade level)",
        main = "Readability across three drafts of one claim",
        names.arg = names(versions))
abline(h = 12, lty = 2)
```

### Revision as a process

First drafts are for the writer; revision is for the reader. The empirical
regularity behind all writing advice is that meaning is discovered, not transcribed:
the act of writing reveals which arrows in @eq-sw-chain are actually weak, and the
first draft's value is largely diagnostic. Productive revision proceeds top-down—
structure before paragraph, paragraph before sentence, sentence before word—because
fixing a comma in a paragraph that will be deleted is wasted effort. A useful
sequence is to first verify that the contribution sentence is present and true,
then that each section answers its one question, then that each paragraph has a
single point announced in its first sentence, and only then to polish prose. The
"reverse outline"—reading the draft and writing in the margin the single claim each
paragraph makes—exposes structural defects (two paragraphs making the same point, a
claim with no supporting paragraph, a paragraph with no claim) that are invisible at
the sentence level.

A final discipline is distance. Prose that seems clear the night it is written is
frequently opaque a week later, when the author has forgotten the unstated
assumptions that made it cohere—and a week-later author is a closer proxy for the
real reader than the night-of author ever is. Where time does not permit distance,
a co-author or colleague reading cold is the next best instrument, and the most
valuable feedback is not "I disagree" but "I got lost here", because confusion
localizes a broken arrow that the author can no longer see.

## Key Takeaways

- A paper is a **reconstructed argument**, not a lab diary: the order of exposition
  is engineered for the reader, and each section answers exactly one question with
  its own default verb tense (@tbl-sw-sections).
- The **effect–mechanism–boundary** architecture answers *whether*, *how*, and *for
  whom* in that order, and the method must change at each stage because the question
  does—quasi-experimental for the average effect, structural equations for the
  pathway, set-theoretic for the configurations (@sec-sw-emb). Put the robustness
  where identification is weakest, and state plainly that identification strength
  declines from stage to stage. The test of whether the later stages are contributions
  rather than decoration is whether a null there would have changed the paper
  [@singh2026opensource].
- A **design-science method paper** hangs on its design framework, which maps goals
  to challenges and gives each challenge exactly one component (@tbl-sw-design-spine).
  It evaluates the method at three levels: model, application, and mechanism. Its
  mechanism evidence is ablation plus a direct check of the property each component
  claims, and its simplest credible rival is the heuristic version of its own idea
  [@wang2026drdl; @xu2026upstar].
- A **theory-building paper** names a construct from data in which hidden behavior was
  forced into the open. It defines the construct from an existing concept, splits it
  into parts a coder can find, states the boundary where it stops applying, sorts its
  forms along one dimension, and derives remedies from the mechanism
  (@tbl-sw-theory-spine). Every headline number should be recomputable from a table in
  the paper [@weiss2026criminal].
- The argument is a chain of claims the reader may refuse to grant
  (@eq-sw-chain); a paper fails at its **weakest arrow**, and most "low
  contribution" rejections are in fact broken arrows—a filled gap or a design that
  cannot license the conclusion.
- Motivate with a **question, not a gap**. The strongest setup assembles two
  established literatures that imply opposite answers, or that block both obvious
  remedies, so that no informed reader can guess the result—human bias and machine
  bias doing exactly that in @tanlamai2026housing (@sec-sw-open-question). Write it so
  both branches are publishable before you know which one you have; remember that a
  counter-intuitive finding raises the evidentiary bar and obligates a real mechanism
  section; and state each literature's position in terms its own authors would sign.
- A contribution is the warranted increment to knowledge $\Delta\mathcal{K}$
  (@eq-sw-contribution); it must be **novel, valid, and important**, and the
  top-4 bar that rises is importance. State the most general claim the evidence
  licenses, and not one inch more.
- The **front end** carries the promise; the discussion must redeem exactly that
  promise. Make the "in this paper, we..." pivot early and state contributions as
  claims, not activities (@fig-sw-funnel).
- Not every paper is hypo-deductive. A **descriptive** paper contributes a
  pattern and names its ceiling; an **abductive** paper reasons from the pattern
  to the best explanation and owes the reader the whole candidate set
  (@eq-sw-abduction). The **PEEBI** structure—priors, establish, evaluate, best
  explanation, implication (@tbl-sw-peebi)—reports that reasoning honestly where
  the deductive template would force a fiction about the order of discovery.
- A **new measure** earns a top-journal contribution when its facts carry a price and
  pose a question they cannot answer alone. When a null outcome gap could be a true
  zero or a real effect masked by selected adoption, a small model disciplined by the
  measured facts, and identified by a moment the headline facts do not use, turns the
  null into a statement about motives: many start-ups advertise a worker-centered
  culture mainly to save on wages [@lee2026startupculture] (@sec-sw-measure-model).
- A **measurement paper** contributes a variable, and its regressions exist to earn
  trust in that variable. Define the construct with a rule, explain why the source
  must contain it, start from a published instrument and print the new one, then climb
  a validation ladder from known groups to independent future outcomes to prices
  (@tbl-sw-measurement-ladder). Check how a count scales with document length before
  choosing a scaling, and validate against human coding as well as outcomes
  [@boustanifar2026intangible] (@sec-sw-measurement).
- **Robustness is rhetoric**: writing the reviewer's objections into the paper
  before submission is the highest-return revision activity, and the R&R response is
  a craft document whose job is to make the editor's decision easy to defend.
- **Clarity is a property of the reader**: measure it (@eq-sw-fog), revise
  top-down from structure to sentence, and use distance or a cold reader to localize
  the arrows you can no longer see are broken.

## Further Reading

For the structure of scientific argument and the discipline of revision, the
classic writing-craft literature is the natural starting point; for the specific
norms of the marketing top-4, the editorials and "from the editor" notes of JM,
JMR, *Marketing Science*, and JCR are the authoritative—and frequently updated—
statements of what each venue rewards. <!-- CITE-NEEDED: editorial/from-the-editor pieces on contribution standards in JM, JMR, Marketing Science, JCR --> The
On the reporting of non-deductive work, @pillai2026peebi is the direct statement
of the PEEBI structure and @pillai2024lovely the companion treatment of what
makes one explanation better than another; @choudhury2026abduction supplies the
design-side account of abduction that the two SMJ papers presuppose. Read
together they are the closest thing the field has to a manual for writing a paper
whose conclusion was discovered rather than predicted.

For the design-science method paper, @hevner2004design set out the guidelines that
IS referees still apply, and @gregor2013positioning explain how to position and state
a design contribution, from an instantiated artifact up to a design theory.
@abbasi2024pathways is the *ISR* editors' statement of what they now expect from
AI-based design research.

The
textual-analysis methods that let us measure the readability of our own and others'
prose are developed in the disclosure literature [@loughran2020; @loughran2020a]
and connect this chapter to the broader treatment of text as data elsewhere in the
book.
